articles.title: Filing: Chip startup Powerlattice raises $86M to ease AI’s power crunch
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Powerlattice , a Vancouver, Wash.-based startup developing chips that cut the power demands of AI processors, has raised $86 million, according to an SEC filing on Friday.

The new funding is nearly triple the $31 million the company had raised when it emerged from stealth last November with a $25 million Series A led by Playground Global and Celesta Capital. Board members include former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger, a general partner at Playground, and Steve Fu of Celesta.
The filing shows Powerlattice is seeking $111 million, with 18 investors participating so far. It does not name the investors or the round. The company declined to comment.
AI chips are drawing so much electricity and throwing off so much heat that data center operators are running into limits on available power and cooling.
“AI is not constrained by capital, it’s constrained by power,” Gelsinger said last year when Powerlattice announced its Series A.

Powerlattice makes what it calls a power delivery chiplet, a small component that sits inside the processor package. Conventional setups route current over long paths to the processor, wasting energy along the way. The company says shortening that path can cut energy use by more than half and boost performance. Powerlattice said last year it was providing engineering samples for GPUs, CPUs and custom accelerators.

CEO Peng Zou , Gang Ren and Sujith Dermal founded the company in 2023. The three are semiconductor veterans whose backgrounds span Qualcomm, Intel and NUVIA, a startup Qualcomm acquired in 2021. Powerlattice also has offices in Chandler, Ariz.; San Jose, Calif.; and Hsinchu, Taiwan.

Earlier this week, Powerlattice announced it had demonstrated what it calls the industry’s first monolithic integrated voltage regulator chiplet, which packs the controller, power transistors and inductors onto a single piece of silicon.

In the test, the chiplet powered a device Powerlattice built to mimic the fast-shifting electrical loads of next-generation AI accelerators. The company says multiple chiplets can be linked to work as one, letting chip designers match the setup to their processors.
“Breaking through the AI power wall requires us to rethink how power reaches the processor,” Zou said in the announcement.

articles.title: Metal fabricator NIC Global to cut 103 jobs near Seattle, move production to Eastern Washington
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Metal fabricator NIC Global plans to close its Woodinville, Wash., plant, eliminating 103 jobs. Declining business from local customers is prompting the company to shift production primarily to Eastern Washington to meet data center-related growth.

The layoffs are scheduled to begin Jan. 18, 2027, with final departures Aug. 31, 2028, according to a notice filed with the Washington Employment Security Department. Affected jobs include assembly, engineering, quality assurance, metal fabrication specialists, and forklift positions.
The building will be returned to its landlord when the lease ends in September 2028.

“This is a sad day for our company. Woodinville is where NIC was formed — three Seattle-area sheet-metal shops brought together under one roof in 2001 — and the people in that building built the foundation of everything NIC is today,” Troy Wood, company president and CEO, said via email.

The 100,000-square-foot site mostly served energy and medical device customers. Wood said the volume of work at the plant has declined while demand has increased in Eastern Washington for customers building power distribution technology needed by data centers.
“NIC is a supplier of sheet-metal fabrications and assemblies, and in our business, being close to our customers is what keeps us competitive,” Wood said.

While most of the work from Woodinville will go to Spokane, and a smaller portion will go to NIC’s Gallatin, Tenn., facility. The company also has manufacturing in Pullman; Chillicothe, Ohio; and Denton, Texas. The work outside of Washington is focused on the heavy truck sector. The company’s headcount is nearly 600.
Laid-off workers will be encouraged to apply for openings at other plants.

There are smaller fabricators remaining in the Seattle area, including JEMCO Components & Fabrications, which provides precision machining and sheet-metal fabrication for customers in medical, aerospace and defense sectors, and QUAL-FAB serving medical and dental customers.
NIC’s legal and financial headquarters will stay in the Woodinville area, where the company plans a new office for its finance, IT, sales and West Coast support teams.
Wood praised the quality and reliability of the Woodinville employees’ work.
“I am grateful to every one of them,” he said, “and especially to those who chose to stay with us through two and a half years of uncertainty and kept doing their jobs with integrity.”

articles.title: Power outage takes down KEXP streaming for Seattle radio station’s worldwide audience
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: KEXP’s website and online streaming were down Friday morning after a power outage hit the Seattle radio station, though its over-the-air broadcast was back and running.

The outage started around midnight, and the station was on and off for a while before it was “knocked offline by a major power outage” between 2 and 3 a.m., said Dashel Schueler, KEXP’s director of marketing and communications. Schueler didn’t know the cause of the outage.
The station’s backup power system, known as an uninterruptible power supply (UPS), also failed.

“There’s no power to the server room infrastructure because the UPS that is supposed to protect all of that gear has failed,” Schueler said. Staff are trying to power critical devices to restore services while they wait for the UPS to be repaired or for a workaround that bypasses it.
There’s no estimate yet for when streaming will return.

Listeners in the Seattle area can tune in at 90.3 FM. The outage affects the KEXP.org stream and the station’s mobile app. KEXP estimates about 175,000 people stream its live broadcast each week, and another 85,000 listen to its shows on-demand.

The outage also took down 92.7 KREV, the station KEXP now owns in the San Francisco Bay Area, which relies on KEXP’s Seattle-based digital infrastructure. Because KEXP’s DJs pick songs live rather than playing a preset playlist, underwriting breaks vary in timing and length, Schueler said. DJs fire the separate Seattle and Bay Area spots manually and at the same time.

KREV was back by around 8:30 to 8:45 a.m., running on a barebones setup KEXP typically uses for remote broadcasts, Schueler said. Listeners may notice some issues while the station gets everything put back together.
Around 7:30 a.m., KEXP DJ John Richards read messages on air from listeners across Seattle who were happy to have the station back — terrestrially at least.
A few posts from listeners on X and Bluesky referenced the streaming outage.

articles.title: Andy Jassy’s prediction: Amazon could have two $1 trillion businesses within a decade
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: No company has ever had a business with $1 trillion in annual revenue. Andy Jassy says Amazon is on a path to have two.

Amazon Web Services and the company’s stores business could both reach that milestone in the next five to 10 years, the Amazon CEO said Thursday in the company’s third-quarter earnings release and on its call with analysts.
It’s “pretty rare” for Jassy to make a projection that far out, Morgan Stanley analyst Brian Nowak observed on the call, asking how he gets there.

Jassy’s answer started with AWS, which is at a $184 billion annual revenue run rate after growing 39% in the third quarter. He expects growth of more than 40% in both 2027 and 2028, and pointed to a $578 billion backlog of contracted AWS revenue.
The largest customers reserve capacity in huge blocks, sometimes as much as a gigawatt at a time, giving Amazon “very good visibility” into 2027, 2028 and part of 2029, he said.
Beyond that, he said, businesses are still early in using AI, the cost of running AI models keeps falling, and new uses keep emerging, such as AI models finding and fixing security flaws.

“You can’t predict with any certainty five to 10 years from now, especially at these types of growth rates,” Jassy said of AWS. “But it’s not a stretch for us to imagine that this could be over a trillion dollar business.”

Jassy’s forecast is a big jump from seven months ago. In March, Jassy told employees that AWS had a chance to reach at least $600 billion in annual revenue within about a decade, double his earlier expectation, according to Reuters .

Amazon’s stores business is bigger than AWS. Sales from Amazon’s online and physical stores totaled $309 billion over the past 12 months, or about $575 billion if Jassy is including third-party seller services and advertising in his trillion-dollar projection. We’ve asked Amazon to clarify.
For comparison, Walmart, the world’s largest retailer, had $713 billion in revenue in its most recent fiscal year.
Whichever numbers he’s using, Jassy said “some folks are sleeping a bit” on how much progress the stores business has made.

Jassy argued that Amazon’s stores business is gaining ground on competitors. Amazon added more than $90 billion in gross sales over the past 12 months, he said, and is adding about twice as much per quarter as its next-largest U.S. competitor.
Units sold are up nearly 15% so far this year, Jassy said. He noted that nearly 80% of retail sales still happen in physical stores, which he expects to shift online over time.
The bold prediction came on a rough day for the company. Amazon shares fell about 6% in after-hours trading after its profit fell short of Wall Street’s expectations .

It’s not going to be cheap to get there. Amazon expects to spend about $220 billion on capital projects this year, mostly for AWS, and Jassy said the company will spend “meaningfully more” in 2027. He said Amazon has “a clear line of sight to attractive financial returns” and is earning back its capital spending faster than before.

The impact is showing up in Amazon’s finances. Its free cash flow, the cash left over after capital spending, was negative $42.4 billion over the past 12 months, compared with positive $14.8 billion a year earlier.

With its spending running ahead of the cash its businesses bring in, Amazon has raised $115 billion through long-term debt this year. Its interest expense more than tripled in the third quarter to $1.7 billion, cutting into its profit.
“We’re in the very early days of this inflection,” Jassy said. “Our strategy is working, and I expect it will for the foreseeable future.”

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: ORCA Survey
articles.author: Mike Orr
paras: The ORCA consortium has a survey asking users about their experiences using ORCA cards and the fare payment system. The survey is open until mid November. The Friday Roundtable column is for short, light, interactive topics, so this is an opportunity to ask readers the same question: how is your experience using ORCA cards and the fare payment system in general?

There are several aspects to consider. There’s tapping an ORCA card, or using a credit card with the new open-payment system for credit cards. Using the readers may be better or worse on Link, regular buses, RapidRide, or Sounder. There’s obtaining the card and refilling it, at a ticket vending machine (TVM), at the MyORCA.com website, or getting a card mailed to you. There’s customer service offices. There’s the fare structure, and free transfers. There’s the times you have to explain the system to visitors or occasional riders at the platform or bus stop when it’s not obvious to them. And probably many other things.
My two biggest issues with ORCA are the time it takes to register a tap, and paying for part of a pass with an e-purse.

When you hold an ORCA card to a reader, the second-generation system takes twice as long to register a tap than the previous system did. So on buses I either have to hold up the line behind me, or tap and leave and assume it will either beep while I’m walking away or it won’t beep and I’ll get a free ride.

The second issue is when you want to split a pass cost between e-purse and a credit card. I switched to e-purse during the pandemic, and back to a pass this year. In the past at TVMs I’ve been able to use the $60 e-purse value for partial payment for the $108 pass, and pay the rest by credit card. I’d then have to do a second credit-card payment to put $10 back into the e-purse for occasional surcharges, because it had no option to take just $50 out of the e-purse and leave the other $10.

This year when I went back to using passes, the TVM wouldn’t even do that. The e-purse option was disabled, so the only choices were credit card or cash. That’s presumably because the e-purse value wasn’t enough for the entire pass. I didn’t want to leave $60 in the e-purse unused forever, so I went to Metro’s customer service office to make the kind of payment split I wanted. It would be nice if the TVMs could do this.

articles.title: Route 40 Upgrades Finally Reach Finish Line, Despite Business Opposition
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Seattle and King County officials cut the ribbon on a suite of upgrades to Metro's workhorse Route 40 on Thursday – transit speed, reliability, and access improvements that have been in the works for the better part of a decade. The changes benefit around 9,000 daily transit riders traveling between Downtown Seattle, Fremont, Ballard, Crown Hill, and Northgate, but several key elements had faced significant opposition from business owners along the route.

Upgrades include three miles of business access and transit (BAT) lanes, targeted at some of the 40's biggest pinch points including stretches through the heart of Ballard, on either side of the Fremont Bridge, and along Westlake Avenue N. Sixteen bus stops were upgraded and more than 6,000 feet of new sidewalks were installed, with new crosswalks and curb ramps up and down the corridor.

"One of the busiest routes in King County – top five actually – has become faster, safer, and easier to use," King County Executive Girmay Zahilay said Thursday. "And for our riders, that means getting a little bit of time back and having a ride that they can count on. This is definitely worth celebrating and sharing gratitude with all of the teams who had so much to do with these improvements, as well as the community members who advocated for this."

Utility work that was able to happen at the same time as construction, including the replacement of 200 feet of water main, stretched out the implementation timeline, as did planning delays and budgetary turmoil. Backers of the 2015 Move Seattle Levy (which funded the project) had hoped to open the Route 40 upgrades as a RapidRide line in 2023, but ultimately scaled back the plan and abandoned the RapidRide branding in 2018 due to a budget crunch and worse federal transit funding outlook under the Trump administration 1.0.

Dedicated road space for buses is what drew the most organized opposition, which continued through the start of construction . In 2021, The Urbanist first reported pushback on the project's initial design coming from Eugene Wasserman, President of the North Seattle Industrial Association.

Wasserman has long been involved in the fight over completing the Missing Link of the Burke-Gilman Trail along Shilshole Way NW through Ballard and was one of the main opponents of the 2015 Levy to Move Seattle, which funded about 30% of the annual budget of the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT). In opposing the Route 40 project, he cited potential impacts on routes used by freight trucks due to reallocating street space.

"It appears to the Maritime/Industrial community that SDOT is willing to sacrifice the viability of maritime/industrial businesses and their employees so that Amazon workers can get to their offices 5 minutes earlier," Wasserman wrote at the time. "Removing the number of traffic lanes the project does will have a substantial impact on our maritime/industrial businesses and will assist in the increasing gentrification of our industrial area."

While that opposition was initially confined to the freight community, it quickly expanded, with business groups in Fremont and Ballard also raising concerns. A 2023 letter signed by Pete Hanning, the head of the Fremont Chamber of Commerce and Mike Stewart, head of the Ballard Alliance, framed the project as out-of-date, citing a reduction in ridership on the Route 40 compared to pre-pandemic levels. Today, the Route 40 is one of the most popular routes in the Metro network, seeing only slightly less usage than the nearby D Line.

"SDOT did not conduct a thorough existing conditions study to identify the specific areas where improvements are needed, let alone the consequences that will result with respect to side-street congestion and overloaded vehicle queues, reliable movement of freight, and increased idling that will result in excessive carbon emissions," the 2023 letter stated.

Two separate traffic analysis studies were conducted on the changes, in response to the issues raised by project opponents and amplified by former Seattle City Council President Sara Nelson. Nelson came out against the bus lanes in 2023 and threatened to kill the transit project through the council budget process in 2024. In 2025, Nelson lost her reelection bid by 25 points to progressive nonprofit leader Dionne Foster.

Business opposition continued into 2025, as some design changes were made to respond to community concerns. SDOT relocated a bus stop location in Fremont and redesigned a new crosswalk at Westlake Avenue N and Halladay Street to reduce impacts on a nearby business. Most notably, the City of Seattle committed to piloting a new concept for the city, a freight-and-bus (FAB) lane along Westlake Avenue N to potentially mitigate some impacts to truck traffic.
Despite those changes, signs reading "Route 40 Plan: We Can Do Better" kept popping up along the route as the project was getting ready to start construction, as organized opposition continued.

Throughout its planning and construction, the project received significant support from multimodal transportation advocates, specifically Ballard Fremont Green Streets (BFG), previously known as Ballard-Fremont Greenways. An email campaign started by the group attempted to counter the opposition, a tactic that certainly helped the Route 40 upgrades to arrive at their ribbon cutting largely unscathed.

Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson, who had been involved in the fight over upgrading the Route 40 as head of the Transit Rider's Union before being elected to lead the city, clearly took joy in being able to mark the occasion.

"These kinds of meaningful improvements matter as they make a difference in the everyday lives of residents of our city, and that is why I've also directed us SDOT to continue this trend to keep making our existing bus routes better at the same time as we launch new ones," Wilson said. "And so, really looking forward to continuing that work."

Zahilay told the crowd Thursday that initial data from Metro on the upgrades shows a 11% improvement in travel time for the Route 40 between Fremont and Ballard, which translates to 90 seconds saved on every bus trip, on average.

"Many of my neighbors and my friends rely on the 40 to work, to visit friends and family, to go to big events, to go shopping," Jason Weill, an advocate with Ballard Fremont Green Streets, said. "One BFG member told me that she commutes using the 40, and she used to deal with long delays, sitting through the bus [waiting] through multiple light cycles. But now the cars that used to block the lane have made way for busses."

But the improvements to the public realm extend beyond benefits to the bus riders themselves, with Lydia Heard of the Fremont Neighborhood Council noting that creating transit lanes has turned Fremont into a more walkable neighborhood.

"The reconfiguration of 35th at Fremont Place has a calming effect and transforms that corner into a more welcoming public space," Heard said. "But perhaps the biggest transformation is where the dedicated bus lane reduced [N] 36th to one general travel lane in each direction. This stretch of street, lined with popular businesses and often teeming with foot traffic, feels quieter and calmer most of the day. It is a much more enjoyable walking experience, and it is easier to cross the street. I think this is what we want for our community."

articles.title: Bellevue's Transportation Funding Debate Pivots Around Safety
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Competing visions for the future of Bellevue's transportation system were put on full display this week at a final public hearing before adoption of the city's next two-year budget. As city leaders contemplate how to utilize several new revenue streams for transportation projects, the big question is how heavily Bellevue will invest in multimodal traffic safety upgrades that reduce deaths and injuries and make it easier to get around without a car.

With a new 0.1% sales tax and a new $20 vehicle license fee likely on deck in Bellevue, the question of utilizing those dollars for safety upgrades had already been top-of-mind during council discussions over the course of this year. But the discussion took on an increased level of urgency after a driver struck and killed 57-year-old James Rupert William Phillips while he was riding his bike at Bellevue Way SE and SE 30th Street on October 15.

Phillips was killed during a planned maintenance closure of the I-90 trail, with a detour directing anyone trying to get between Bellevue and Mercer Island to city streets. According to an initial police report, Phillips, a Newcastle resident, was crossing Bellevue Way when he was struck in one of Bellevue Way's inside lanes. The driver remained at the scene, Bellevue Police Department reported .

Crossing Bellevue Way in this spot, which doesn't include any crossing infrastructure, would be a tempting choice for anyone trying to get to the westbound I-90 trail without having to backtrack from all the way from 112th Avenue NE.

While decisions around the trail detour rested with King County as part of the North Mercer Island/Enatai Sewer Upgrade Project , the incident has thrown a spotlight on conditions on Bellevue's arterial streets.

Earlier this month, Bellevue councilmembers got a full breakdown on potential funding scenarios that would allocate more than $100 million in new funding across the Eastside's largest city over the next decade. Under the most ambitious scenario, which includes the 0.1% sales tax on top of the vehicle license fees, bicycle and pedestrian safety projects would see 28% of the city's total transportation spending through 2036. Neighborhood safety projects including traffic calming would see an additional 13%.

At Tuesday's hearing, councilmembers heard from Bellevue residents, workers, and visitors about whether to tweak or maintain those funding levels. Over recent weeks, signs have been popping up around Bellevue reading "no car tab tax" and "don't raise sales taxes." A fair share of speakers at the hearing told the council that new revenue tools should go to the voters, but most touching on transportation urged the city to stick to this new proposed baseline or go even further.

"I appreciate, value, and am very grateful for Bellevue adopting Vision Zero goals. We clearly need to do more," Bellevue resident Elaine White said, referencing the tragic Bellevue Way incident. "Please adopt scenario 3 in the 2027-2028 transportation budget. It funds more speed cameras, more improvements for vulnerable users and slower speeds. Yes, it will cost each household an additional $6 a month. Fellow residents of Bellevue, what might the life of your loved one be worth protecting? I'm happy to pay $6 per month for safer streets."

One area of emphasis was the "major projects" category, which would see most of the $40 million in new spending go toward getting a $74.8 million roadway project through the BelRed neighborhood across the finish line. The Spring Boulevard Zone 3 project would reconnect a segment of the street grid with sidewalks and protected bike lanes, but at an enormous cost – bringing a roadway through one of the neighborhood's only planned park spaces.

"In the last two and a half years since the light rail station was opened, nothing was made to improve pedestrian or bicycle access to the light rail station. During the last five years, we asked repeatedly for mid-block crossing on our street, and we heard no results," Crossroads resident Alex Kon said. "While then transportation department for years can't find money to fix those glaring safety and accessibility gaps, it suggests to spend $75 million dollars to build new arterial road nobody is asking for, and to add insult to injury, this road will go right through the park, so it will split into halves instead of improving connectivity for people who live there or who visit the park."

The Grand Connection Crossing , Bellevue's plan to construct a bike and pedestrian bridge across I-405 between Downtown and the Wilburton neighborhood, was also a target of public comments. While the crossing is set to receive around 10% of revenue from the sales tax increase, those dollars had been set to come from Bellevue's general fund, freeing up dollars that can be spent more broadly.

"In this budget, our central request is to keep the Grand Connection Crossing funded and moving forward," Patrick Bannon, President and CEO of the Bellevue Downtown Association. "Connecting Downtown, Wilburton, Eastrail will make it easier to reach jobs, businesses, homes, places to shop, places to eat. It will help attract the next generation of private investment and support the next wave of housing growth in our city."
While the city's business community is fully on board with the idea of building the Grand Connection Crossing, the project has its detractors.

"Responsible government should address current problems such as traffic congestion first, which would be [a] much more reasonable cost than the current proposal. Instead, the most pressing concerns of the transportation department, from the beginning, the past several years, seems to have been on serving cyclists by narrowing lanes and later by building the Grand Connection," Bridle Trails resident Anne Coughlin said. "It seems that the few blocks from 112 to 116[th] are a great barrier to those who wish to cross it on bicycle, as though it were the 3.6 million miles separating sub-Saharan Africa from the north, the Himalayas, or the Amazonian rainforest."

But the Grand Connection Crossing is far from the only transportation project that the business community is advocating for. Tony Sprague, Public Policy Manager for the Bellevue Chamber of Commerce, noted that their group's support for the funding package is contingent on no reductions for "vehicular capacity" projects, and has also requested that additional revenue beyond current sales tax projections be put into the "underperforming intersection" fund.

The vehicle mobility program already includes three planned intersection widenings, at SE 8th St and 114th Ave SE, NE 12th St and 116th Ave NE, and 148th Ave NE and NE 8th St, for a total cost of $24.5 million. That's more funding for three projects than the entire neighborhood mobility program would receive in new funding over the course of a full decade.

Whether any additional funding can be diverted into the types of transportation modes that Bellevue will need to grow sustainably over the coming decades – walking, biking and transit – remains to be seen in the coming weeks. Following council deliberations on November 3 and 10, a finalized budget is expected to be adopted by the Bellevue Council on November 17.

articles.title: From gunfire to combative arrests: How the Seattle Police Department talks about East Precinct crime is changing
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: (Source: CHS analysis of SPD Significant Incident Reports )

As Capitol Hill crime trends are shifting as part of City Hall priorities to increase public safety downtown, the way the public is informed about the Seattle Police Department’s day to day enforcement, arrests, and challenges across the city and in the East Precinct is also changing.

CHS reported here this summer on a key shift as SPD and Seattle Fire have now mostly fully encrypted their dispatch and emergency radio transmissions, cutting off real-time public and scanner access to tactical and operational channels.
Other public channels documenting 911 incidents in the city are also shifting.

One suddenly more important outlet with the radio channel near-blackout are SPD’s Significant Incident Reports . Prepared by each precinct for daily command briefings, the department has regularly published a selected stream of SIR updates for over six years now after beginning the practice following the onset of the pandemic and the civil unrest surrounding CHOP .

The stream of briefs signed-off on and approved by precinct commanders for publication provide information on individual incidents and arrests. They are also revealing of shifting priorities in information at SPD.

While the Seattle Police Department has drastically curtailed SIR public blotter updates citywide, East Precinct’s totals have taken an opposite path, not only expanding its share of published reports, but transforming the precinct’s Significant Incident Reports stream into a platform focused on officer hazards and physical resistance during arrests.

Across the department, blotter publication has slowed to all-time lows in 2026. Citywide postings dropped nearly 25% year-to-date, falling from a 2021 peak of 5.4 daily incident reports to just 2.4. The South and Southwest precincts drive much of this pullback, paring down their posts to focus primarily on gunfire and shell casing recoveries, with shootings accounting for around 40% of their recent posts.
East Precinct moved in the opposite direction. From 2021 through 2023, East accounted for just 14.9% of all citywide SIR entries, ranking last among SPD’s five precincts.
That came even as downtown enforcement pushed crime eastward , with Capitol Hill recording 780 additional offenses by 2025 and passing downtown for the city’s highest raw crime count.
In 2025 and 2026, East’s share of the blotter also surged — to 20.8%, overtaking both South and Southwest. A bigger change in the East reports is their nature.

Instead of cataloging major neighborhood violence — confirmed gunfire reports dropped from 28.3% of East entries during 2021–2023 down to 16.9% recently — the blotter has shifted toward documenting the occupational hazards and physical friction officers encounter while making arrests.

East now leads the entire city in publicizing physical threats to personnel. Over 12% of recent East posts, peaking at nearly 14% in 2025, detail suspects physically fighting officers during handcuffing, spitting in officers’ faces, brandishing weapons at patrol, or facing felony assault and obstruction charges. These physical confrontations frequently emerge during lower-level disorder calls, including retail trespass, public urination, and crisis detentions.
Arrests are also highlighted. Reports emphasizing suspect custody leaped from 36.3 to 46.1%.

Even as monthly crime across Capitol Hill and First Hill began cooling in late summer 2026, the East Precinct information flow has held firm, making the precinct’s SIR updates a record of enforcement hazards and showcasing the combative arrests and physical resistance officers face.

As for what is happening day to day across the neighborhoods of the East Precinct, sources like the Seattle Fire real-time 911 logs remain. A growing array of for–pay, non-public services like the Citizen app are also flowering. Citizen was originally launched as “Vigilante” and is backed by prominent Silicon Valley venture capital firms, high-profile angel investors, and growth funds if you have any question about the goals behind it.

As Seattle’s public safety communications contract behind encrypted radios and reduced blotter output, the day-to-day picture of policing in the East Precinct could largely become a reflection of command selection. While commercial apps monetize access to 911 monitoring, SPD’s official updates have narrowed their lens.

The city’s news gatherers have weathered change before and CHS is finding new ways to keep up with — and dig up — crime and emergency news. We also have access to a unique and powerful resource — you:

articles.title: Coming to Capitol Hill’s Broadway ballot drop box: music, dancing, and civic duty
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Now you know what happens inside the box (Image: King County Elections)
Voters heading to Capitol Hill heading into Tuesday’s Election Night can turn civic duty into a community celebration before Washington’s 8 PM voting deadline on November 3.

articles.title: Seattle launches 4% small business loan revamp — with a boost for spots like Capitol Hill’s Ooink to sell its ramen nationwide
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: The City of Seattle has revamped its Small Business Capital Access Program to deliver fixed 4% interest rate loans to local entrepreneurs facing rising operational costs and predatory lending risks.

Announced by Mayor Katie Wilson , the Seattle Office of Economic Development, and nonprofit partner Grow America this week, the updated initiative enables qualified small business owners to secure up to $350,000 in financing with locked-in, lifetime interest rates. Funds can cover essential day-to-day overhead, including payroll, rent, utilities, and supplies.

Formerly the National Development Council, Grow America is a national nonprofit that partners with local governments and community lenders to deliver affordable financing, technical assistance, and investment capital to small businesses and underserved communities.

Six participating community lenders, consisting of local credit unions and Community Development Financial Institutions will administer the loans. The streamlined system is hoped to also limit paperwork from borrowers; lenders automatically process the CAP application once a business qualifies.
City officials emphasize that the program levels the playing field for historically underserved business owners navigating inflation, rent spikes, and supply-chain pressures.

Since launching in 2021, CAP has distributed nearly $7 million across 331 Seattle businesses, unlocking more than $27.8 million in affordable financing to keep neighborhood commercial districts vibrant and storefronts open and thriving.

Local recipients include 20-year-old Capitol Hill noodle bar Ooink which tapped the program to manage overhead and fund expansion into packaged nationwide distribution, while in the Central District, the Urban League of Metropolitan Seattle has served as a technical assistance navigator, helping historically underserved and BIPOC entrepreneurs prepare financials and secure financing through participating mission-based lenders like Craft3 , Business Impact NW, and Community Capital Development .

articles.title: Seattle Wants to Help RV Residents by Banning Their Homes
articles.author: By Dr. Graham Pruss
paras: Seattle’s City Council just voted to spend $5 million helping people who live in vehicles—while ultimately banning RVs overnight from the city and making it harder for people to keep these homes. On October 20, Councilmember Dan Strauss’s Vehicle Resident Assistance Program (VRAP) passed as a legislative package. VRAP now moves to Mayor Katie Wilson to accept, veto, or ignore.

These are separate policies, and should be considered separately. Mayor Wilson should sign CB 121282 to support outreach and assistance, veto CB 121283’s punitive parking rules, and veto CB 121280 unless its redefinition of junk-vehicles protects lived-in homes. Seattle can fund help without making another community homeless.

The number of vehicle residents who called Seattle home has been increasing for decades, from 544 people in 2006 to 3,372 by 2018 . A 2026 UW report showed that the number of people in smaller vehicles has nearly tripled since 2022, while those in larger vehicles have reduced dramatically.

I began working with vehicle residents in 2009, coordinating a community meal under the Ballard Bridge and advocating with others to establish Seattle’s first safe parking program. From 2013 to 2015, I was employed by that program as the city’s only designated outreach worker to vehicle residents. I met shipwrights, fishing crews, construction workers, retirees, and families who bought older RVs because rent was out of reach. They parked near work, medical care, food, bathrooms, family, and friends.

Our safe parking program offered space on a list for our consistently full lots in churches across North Seattle. We helped people maintain their position on housing waitlists for years. I delivered water, snacks, and warnings from the police of impending ticketing, tows, and impounds. I saw entire city blocks of overnight parking restriction signs and concrete “ecoblocks” installed in the immediate aftermath of these sweeps. I watched homes disappear, often with medicine, paperwork, photographs, and heirlooms inside. Some were auctioned cheaply; others scrapped.

For decades, Seattle’s vehicle residents have navigated a legal landscape that determines when they can park their homes. A 1979 city law required oversized vehicles to park overnight on industrial streets. “No Parking 2-5 AM” signs were installed throughout those industrial zones, increasing the density of RVs on the remaining streets with overnight parking.

As parking options narrowed, residents gathered together for security, repairs, and mutual aid. They formed communities on industrial streets, areas with few toilets, water taps, or trash cans and where rodents chewed engine wires and hoses.

Encampments grew during the pandemic when an RV offered room to isolate while much of the city sheltered indoors. Businesses and public buildings closed, bathrooms and shelter access became more difficult, and service providers pulled their outreach teams from the streets to protect frontline workers.

RV residents clustered in the few remaining legal spaces for safety and mutual support. They shared resources, watched over each other’s possessions, helped repair vehicles, and created communities. Many congregated in growing encampments because they had no other choice.

When businesses reopened, the sweeps resumed, pushing people from familiar parking places into existing RV clusters, then displacing them to fewer and fewer remaining streets. The resulting overcrowding—often without basic sanitation—became justification for still more removals.
After years of pushing RV residents into increasingly crowded and underserved spaces, Seattle now proposes to eliminate the few places they have left.

Some of the VRAP funding is welcome. But the proposed rules will effectively ban RVs from Seattle. By packaging these together, Strauss’ proposal was supported by those it would fund. Meanwhile, it has been denounced by lived experience advocacy groups across the region and country.

Under CB 121283, only registered vehicle owners identified in a one-time citywide census could apply for RV parking permits. Someone who moves into an RV afterward—or visits Seattle to work, see family, or seek medical care—would have no route to a permit. Unpermitted motorhomes and travel trailers could park on public streets for only two hours, and not at all between midnight and 6 a.m.

Permitted residents could park overnight only in assigned industrial areas; daytime parking would remain subject to posted restrictions. They would have to stay engaged with city-approved caseworkers and on waitlists for safe parking, shelter, vehicle storage, or housing. Six refusals of “appropriate shelter” could cost them the permit, though the bill leaves that term for an implementation workgroup to define. Calling someone service resistant doesn’t make the offered service appropriate. Coercion is not compassion.

While the proposed $5 million investment from existing city funds could make a meaningful difference, there are no plans to provide alternative parking for RVs that meets the scale of need. The parking restrictions are scheduled for April 30, 2027, with enforcement beginning July 31 if enacted.

VRAP’s carrot and stick approach reflects a broader shift toward displacing vehicle residents rather than accommodating their homes. Seattle is joining a crackdown on RVs throughout the Western States. In 2025, San Francisco imposed a similar two-hour limit on large vehicles, with one-time offered permits. Santa Cruz and San Diego have similar Oversized Vehicle Ordinances that ban RVs overnight from the majority of their streets.

Kirkland restricted wide RVs on city streets this fall. On the day of the Seattle VRAP vote, King County Councilmember Reagan Dunn proposed a motion seeking new parking restrictions on unincorporated roads, including proposals for booting vehicles with repeated unpaid citations.
Every jurisdiction that closes its streets shifts the pressure to the next, further limiting where people can live.

“I’m not homeless, this is my home.” I’ve heard those words more times than I can remember. People use RVs as emergency shelter, transitional housing, and long-term homes. An RV occupied for years can be more stable than an overnight shelter bed. Many emergency shelters separate people from their partners, pets, possessions, and privacy. People rely on RVs as housing in Seattle because more permanent options that meet these needs are inaccessible.

They include seasonal workers, seniors on fixed incomes, veterans staying near VA care, and families keeping children in school. Some identify as homeless; many do not. Many use RVs as stop-gap housing, and many more have chosen a mobile life. Their reasons differ, but a vehicle may preserve work, health care, family ties, and a measure of control.
Stripping away people’s assets will not end homelessness.

Seattle should address fire hazards, waste, and sanitation. But the answer to missing toilets and water is providing toilets and water—not taking away the roof over someone’s head. Fund safe overnight lots, 24-hour RV parking with services, and longer-term sites with utilities, all designed with residents and offered voluntarily.
Seattle cannot tow its way out of a housing crisis.
Dr. Graham Pruss is a University of Washington-trained anthropologist, former Seattle safe-parking outreach worker, and executive director of the National Vehicle Residency Coalition.

articles.title: Black sorority organizes public policy forum with WA leaders
articles.author: Paris Jackson
paras: On a crisp Saturday morning, Washington politicians and community members gathered inside an auditorium at Highline College in Des Moines for a discussion on the pain points facing the state

The Seattle and Tacoma graduate chapters of the historic Black sorority Alpha Kappa Alpha held the non-partisan public policy forum with Democratic elected officials and a representative from the Washington Secretary of State’s Office.
Organizers said they reached out to Republican leaders as well.

“We reached out to multiple political officials and their counterparts. Some declined many did not respond, or already had a conflict in their schedule. This is for both majority parties,” said Antaknea Majors, a Alpha Kappa Alpha Sorority, Inc. Public Policy Forum Committee Member.
Dr. Rotonya Carr, a member of the Delta Upsilon Omega Chapter of AKA, says the event is important for civic engagement.

“ People need to know that the people who we elect and who are working for us on behalf of Washington State, are our leaders. They are accessible to us. They are no different than you or me, but they have a very special job to do. So having events like this that bring them here to our community, where we can engage in direct dialogue, is so critically important. And to have it as a nonpartisan event, also very important,” Carr said.

At the mid-October event, the panel included Washington Attorney General Nick Brown, State Representative Edwin Obras, and voter education specialist from the Washington Secretary of State’s Office Sarah Spikes. State Representative Jamila Taylor served as moderator.

Washington Governor Bob Ferguson wasn’t there, but sent a video message, in which he spoke about his efforts to protect Washingtonians’ healthcare after the federal government last year passed H.R. 1, known as the ‘Big Beautiful Bill.’
Ferguson said it cut more than $3 billion from the state’s Medicaid funding for the upcoming biennium.
He said it impacts about 600,000 residents, who are facing the potential loss of their Medicaid benefits through the state’s program.

“In response to all this, what I really consider to be a morally bankrupt policy, I signed an executive order that seeks to do everything we can to keep as many Washingtonians as possible on their health insurance,” Ferguson said.
Washington voter and attendee Kara Sims said healthcare is a major concern as her parents age.

“ As a person who's in the sandwich generation, one issue that's really important to me is healthcare. Having a conversation with my mom yesterday and understanding the trade-offs that she's evaluating with regards to Medicaid, it's complicated. And I think about my parents, who are seniors, and for them to navigate this,” Sims said.

Another topic discussed at the forum was the state’s vote by mail system, which has been under attack through Executive Orders from the Trump administration. Washington is one of many states that have gone to court to protect the legal rights of voters.
Brown said his office has sued the President over 80 times in his 22 months as attorney general. Brown said that’s about a suit nearly every week.

“It saddens me a little bit that so much of our work is defending Americans from their President,” Brown said. “Over the course of the past year, we have been defending our state, and our laws, and the United States Constitution against an illegal, unconstitutional, un-American power grab from this President. Starting with an attempt to change the date by which we count ballots.”
State Representatives Taylor and Obras stressed the importance of finding common ground with their constituents.

“There is not a single district in Washington state that is majority Black,” Taylor said. Then, she asked Obras, “So how do you navigate coalitions with folks that may not come from the same ethic community, but they share your values?”

“Sure. I think laying your values on the table is first and foremost,” Obras replied. “Cause what that does, it naturally brings people together. When you are an elected official, there are a lot of opportunities to build those bridges. I can’t say enough - emphasis how important it is to be accessible, do outreach, and engage.”
For West Seattle resident Howard Brantley, affordability is a major issue for his family.

“I have a 29-year-old that lives here, lives in the Seattle area at the same time too. I think my biggest concern is affordability. And that continues to come up, especially here in Washington. With the rising cost of housing, rising cost, again of groceries,” said Brantley.
Spikes shared election reminders and highlighted facts about voting in the state, such as that Washington is among just a few states that produce a voter pamphlet.
She urged voters to use drop boxes instead of the postal service to ensure their ballot arrives in time, due to postmark changes.

“We are in a great position in Washington. I've lived in South Carolina, I've lived in Georgia, and I've lived in Florida,” Brantley said. “And one of the things that Sarah Spikes talked about is having that voter pamphlet. Use that voter pamphlet. Be informed of what's on the ballot, who's on the ballot, and why they're on the ballot before you take that right. Please vote, because this election is so critical.”
To check your voter registration status and track your ballot go to votewa.gov .

articles.title: This is the hard lesson from Israel’s election: to stop national populists, you can’t play by gentlemen’s rules | Jonathan Freedland
articles.author: Jonathan Freedland in Tel Aviv
paras: The opposition can’t win unless they join forces with Arab parties. Benjamin Netanyahu knows this, and will use every ruse to stay in power

It’s less an election result than a philosophical puzzle: what happens when a win contains a loss, a loss contains a win and the two collide? That’s the question posed by the confused and confusing outcome of this week’s Israeli election, one that, despite its murky uncertainty, offers clear, sharp lessons – both for that country and for those locked in combat with nationalist populists across the globe.

Start with the result that has simultaneously handed Benjamin Netanyahu a devastating defeat and a strong chance of staying on as prime minister, extending a run that has seen him lead Israel, on and off, for more than 19 of the past 30 years. The defeat is clear enough. At a stroke, his parliamentary majority was wiped out. Before Tuesday, the parties that together comprised his ruling coalition controlled 68 of the Knesset’s 120 seats: that tally has now shrunk to just 53 , far short of the 61 seats needed for power. That’s a loss in anybody’s language.
Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

Becoming an author in my late 50s was unexpected, the result of my daughter Hallie’s own existential anxiety in her early 20s.

Fearing my untimely demise, she begged me to write down advice that would cover all of life’s bases going forward. I agreed, but put the project off for years; it wasn’t until she cornered me with a laptop on vacation that I gave in. She asked countless questions, and I found, to my surprise, that I had plenty to say. Hallie helped shape the manuscript, and then spent a year painting its warmly emotional gouache illustrations.
I lost a parent (or other loved one, including spouse or beloved pet) and your book helped me through.

articles.title: Ghost in the machine: how AI is haunting the search for the supernatural
articles.author: AW Ohlheiser
paras: Ghost hunting has changed in recent years due to AI chatbots, and paranormal enthusiasts are concerned

Ghost hunting is a tech-heavy pursuit. When Amy Waine and Jarrad Cutting investigate haunted locations, they’re loaded up with software of their own design, such as an app that assigns signals from a phone’s sensors to different words in a database. In the age of ChatGPT, the ghost-hunting pair is probing the world of AI. They describe one of their latest inventions, an app called GhostTube Seer , as “the world’s first AI Ghost Hunting tool”. In the hands of paranormal investigators, scientific tools like EMF meters (used to detect electromagnetic fields) are repurposed to identify changes and anomalies that they believe indicate supernatural activity. Seer is, in many ways, simply an expansion of that practice, another way to scan an empty room and believe that something may be there. The app, which requires a paid monthly subscription, has more than 1m downloads, according to its Google Play store listing .

But for others in the ghost hunting world, AI is an unwelcome presence. Since the release of ChatGPT in 2022, AI-generated ghost stories and images of the supernatural have flooded online spaces, so much so that popular forums like the r/Nosleep subreddit , meant for scary stories, have implemented a strict policy against AI-generated material.

paras: After improbable election victory, the unconventional grassroots movement says it will prioritise dismissal of corrupt officials

In Belgrade’s Pioneers Park, just across from the national assembly, a small crowd craned their necks to listen. One woman held aloft a placard reading “Love prevailed for the people and Serbia”. With a bouquet of media microphones in front of them, members of the Student List, the direct democracy movement that won an improbable but decisive victory in Sunday’s election, gathered under the trees.

Having spent days bathing in the euphoria of their unexpected triumph , the candidates’ focus was now clear: the cleaning up of the rotten institutions that had increasingly blighted the lives of Serbs over the 14 years of government by the populist leader Aleksandar Vučić and his Serbian Progressive party (SNS). They called for the dismissal of many senior law enforcement officials, among them the chiefs of the criminal police, the paramilitary gendarmerie and an anti-terrorism unit.

articles.title: From 18th-century false ballots to the second JFK and double Dan Sullivans, a brief history of spoiler candidates and the unsuccessful legal challenges to them
articles.author:
<name>Drew Kurlowski, Associate Professor of Political Science, Coastal Carolina University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/drew-kurlowski-2312625"/>
paras: Less than a week before Election Day, The New York Times reported that people with links to Alaska Democrat Mary Peltola’s U.S. Senate campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee had recruited a candidate to the race whose name is nearly identical to that of the incumbent Republican senator, Dan Sullivan, whom Peltola was challenging. The plan aimed to siphon votes from the incumbent senator and help Peltola win, according to the reporting.

The story has driven calls for prosecutions , lawsuits and state action . But as a political scientist who studies election law , I can say that the spoiler candidate is one of the oldest tricks in the American campaign toolbox, and the law has rarely touched it.
For most of the 1800s, American elections were conducted with ballots designed and printed by the parties. There were no official ballots printed by the state.

In those days, the addition of a rival name to a party ballot by an insidious printer could swing countless votes to the opposing party. The tactic was well known, and voters were often warned to look out for the “ Spurious Ticket .”
By the 1890s, the government-printed ballot had gained widespread adoption and ended the practice of counterfeit tickets. But that would not be enough to deter those who wanted to deceive voters.
As observers in Alaska have noted , recruiting candidates with similar or identical names is not a new move.

In John F. Kennedy’s first congressional primary, his opponent was a city councilor named Joseph Russo. An aide to Kennedy reportedly paid a janitor with the same name to enter the race. The real Russo complained, but in the end, Kennedy took more votes in the 1946 race than the Russos combined.

Eight years later, the name Kennedy worked the other way, when a Gillette stockroom supervisor named John Francis Kennedy , no relation, was elected as a Democrat to the position of treasurer and receiver-general of Massachusetts, owing in large part to the familiarity of his name. Names can move votes, so namesakes can be worth recruiting.
Some spoiler candidates are not necessarily meant to win votes. Sometimes they are there to amplify a message.

In 1978, Republican Carroll Campbell was running for an open House seat in upstate South Carolina. His opponent was Max Heller, the mayor of Greenville and a Jewish refugee from Nazi-occupied Austria.

Days before the election, Don Sprouse, an independent running for office for the first time, held a press conference and declared that Heller was unfit for office as he had “not made clear to the voters he is not a Christian” and was “not as qualified to represent the Christian people.”

Although Campbell condemned the remarks and Sprouse received only 1,693 votes, Heller lost the race. The allegations, still unproven, of Sprouse being a “stalking-horse” for Campbell only surfaced years later, but they continued to dog Campbell when he ran for governor in 1986.
Sprouse wasn’t going to spoil the election with the votes he could win, but he could be a spoiler with his message, an antisemitic appeal that Campbell would not make directly.
A different type of ballot shenanigan skips the recruitment and simply puts candidates on the ballot.

This was the case in 2010 when two Oakland County, Michigan, Democratic officials put candidates on the ballot under the Tea Party label in three races. The candidates didn’t even know they were running.
In this case, the law did come back to bite. The county party chair and operations director were charged with perjury and forgery , but the crime was forging signatures, not their strategy.

Some state election codes specifically discuss false declarations or forged election paperwork, but many don’t contemplate this type of scheme. Forgery and perjury, however, are illegal across the country, and it’s almost impossible to put an unwitting person on the ballot without one or the other.

In Alaska, this tactic can be used cheaply. There is no petition requirement to get on the ballot, just a $100 fee. Moreover, the parties can’t vet candidates in the primary. The state’s unique top-four primary system lets candidates choose their own party label.
The saga of Daniel J. Sullivan , the schoolteacher known as “Petersburg Sullivan” because of where he lives , and Sen. Dan S. Sullivan goes back longer than recent revelations.

Petersburg Sullivan filed to run as a Republican in the Senate race just three days before the deadline; state officials tried to bar him from the ballot. In June a judge said there was nothing in Alaska law to prevent him from appearing on the ballot, and the state Supreme Court subsequently agreed.

Since he couldn’t be removed, the state Division of Elections took unusual steps on their ballot design to help distinguish the two candidates. They listed Sen. Dan S. Sullivan as a Republican, marking him as the incumbent, and left Daniel J. Sullivan without a party designation . This had not been done for previous incumbents in at least a decade.

Assuming there is no forgery of documents with an unwitting and unwilling spoiler candidate, there is little the law can do. History shows us that the real legal exposure in these cases usually lies where it most often does in politics: money.

In a 2020 Miami, Florida, race, a former state senator turned political operative was convicted of three felonies related to efforts to recruit and pay a decoy candidate with the same surname as the Democratic incumbent. In another Florida case, a local Republican Party chair was convicted in connection with a scheme to plant a progressive alternative to siphon votes from the Democratic candidate. In both cases the prosecutions focused on campaign finance crimes, not simply on putting the spoilers on the ballot.

The state of Washington is an outlier, where it is a felony to run under a rival’s surname if the intent is to confuse voters . In 2024, two Bob Fergusons were recruited by conservative activist Glen Morgan to run for governor against state Attorney General Bob Ferguson. Both opted to drop out of their race under threat of prosecution.

There is nothing comparable to these laws in Alaska, however, and whether laws like this could prevent this type of thing in a federal election is still untested. Under the Supreme Court’s decision in U.S. Term Limits v. Thornton in 1995, states cannot add their own qualifications for Congress.

The advice from 1860 – “Watch your tickets on election day. There’s a scheme on foot …” – when newspapers urged voters to read their tickets before casting their vote, is still relevant long after the demise of the party ticket. It is unlikely that the law can solve this problem, because to do so would be to wade into the First Amendment waters of why people run for office. Regulating thought and intention is a dangerous proposition under the Constitution.
The old answer is the best one. Self-government depends less on clever rules and more on citizens paying attention. Read your ballots!

articles.title: Allegheny County is reassessing every property – here’s how your tax bill is calculated now
articles.author:
<name>Elizabeth Jane Beckett-Camarata, Professor of Public Administration, Penn State</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/elizabeth-jane-beckett-camarata-2764336"/>
paras: Allegheny County will undergo a countywide reassessment of every property it taxes for the first time since 2012. A county judge ordered the reassessment in August 2026, requiring the work to begin by July 1, 2027, and finish within five years .

The goal is to bring property values in line with today’s market. That could shift the tax burden among property owners across the county. State anti-windfall rules may require local governments to lower their tax rates after a reassessment to ensure they balance and equalize the tax reassessments. Individual bills may go up or down.

For many homeowners, property taxes are confusing. Terms such as assessment, millage rate and school district tax come up often, but taxpayers may not know what they mean or how each one affects their annual tax bill.
In Pittsburgh, property taxes pay for schools, parks, libraries, public safety and other local services.
I research and teach government finance at Penn State Harrisburg , including a course on state and local taxation. Here’s a plain-language guide to how Pittsburgh’s property taxes work.
The first concept is the property assessment. Allegheny County’s Office of Property Assessments gives every property an assessed value. That value is the basis for calculating property taxes.

An assessed value isn’t necessarily what a home would sell for today. Some places, such as Philadelphia , assess property at full market value. Other jurisdictions assess property at a set percentage of market value. In Cook County, Illinois , which includes Chicago, homes are assessed at 10% of their market value. That doesn’t mean Chicago-area homeowners pay less. When assessments are a smaller share of market value, tax rates are set higher to raise the same amount of money. Allegheny County assesses at full value, but it uses what properties were worth in 2012. The court-ordered reassessment is meant to close the gap between those 2012 values and today’s market.

Allegheny County’s 14-year gap would be unusual almost anywhere else. Pennsylvania is the only state that doesn’t require counties to reassess on a regular schedule, while most states do so at least every six years. Within Pennsylvania, though, Allegheny is far from the worst: Butler County hasn’t reassessed since 1969 .
Homeowners can look up their assessment on the county’s real estate portal .

Once a property has an assessed value, each local government applies a millage rate to figure out the tax owed. One mill equals $1 of tax for every $1,000 of assessed value. A home assessed at $100,000 has 100 units of $1,000 in value.
Pittsburgh property owners pay property taxes to three government entities: Allegheny County, the City of Pittsburgh and Pittsburgh Public Schools. Each one sets its own millage rate .

For 2026, the city’s general rate is 9.67 mills. The city also charges 0.5 mill for parks and 0.25 mill for libraries. Pittsburgh Public Schools charges 10.457 mills, and Allegheny County charges 6.43 mills.
Together, those rates add up to 27.307 mills. For a city home assessed at $100,000, that comes to about $2,731 a year before any exemptions or discounts.

The county’s property tax worksheet and the county treasurer’s millage rate page list current rates. These rates are set each year, and all of them will be cut when reassessed values take effect, since the law requires rates to drop as total values rise.

School taxes are often the largest share of a homeowner’s property tax bill. In Pennsylvania, property taxes are a major source of revenue for public schools . They help fund salaries for teachers, updates and maintainance for buildings, transportation, and technology and educational programs.

School tax rates vary widely across Allegheny County. Pittsburgh Public Schools charges 10.457 mills, well below the suburban districts around it. North Allegheny , one of the lowest-taxing suburban districts, charges about 20.4 mills for the 2026-27 school year. Two of the highest are Mt. Lebanon at about 32 mills and Penn Hills at about 32.6 mills. The county treasurer publishes a full list of school district rates .
Some homeowners qualify for programs that lower their tax bills.

The Allegheny County Homestead exemption, known as Act 50 , cuts $18,000 from the assessed value of a qualified, owner-occupied, primary residence property’s county taxes. There’s no income limit: Any homeowner who lives in the property as their primary residence qualifies. A home assessed at $100,000 is taxed on just $82,000, which saves about $116 a year. Enrolling in Act 50 also automatically applies Pittsburgh’s $15,000 exemption , which covers the parks and library levies, and a larger Pittsburgh Public Schools exemption that is set each year. Applications for this exemption are due March 1 and need to be filed only once.

The senior citizen tax relief program, known as Act 77 , takes another 30% off county taxes for homeowners who are at least 60, have household incomes of $30,000 or less and have owned and lived in their home for at least 10 years. For a qualifying senior with that $100,000 home, the county bill would drop from about $527 to about $369.

Homeowners who believe their assessment is too high can appeal their assessment to the county’s Board of Property Assessment Appeals and Review . Filing is free; appeals can be submitted online, by email or in person.

Appeals are filed the year before the tax year they affect. The appeal window for 2027 bills closed Sept. 1, 2026. The next window, for 2028 bills, is expected to run from July 1 to Sept. 1, 2027, around the time the reassessment is set to begin.

At an appeal hearing, homeowners can argue their property’s value using either 2012 prices or today’s market. Recent sales of similar homes nearby can help show whether an assessment is out of line. The board can lower the assessment, leave it as is or raise it.

Pittsburgh property taxes come down to two elements: the property’s assessed value and the millage rates set by the county, the city and the school district. Understanding how these elements work together can help homeowners read and comprehend their tax bills and better plan for one of the biggest ongoing costs of owning a home, next to the mortgage payment.

That understanding will matter more as the reassessment gets underway. When new values take effect, some homeowners will see their share of the tax burden rise and others will see it fall. The direction depends on how their property’s value has changed compared with changes of other similar properties since 2012.
Read more of our stories about Pittsburgh and Pennsylvania .

articles.title: Why achieving your goals can leave you feeling so empty
articles.author:
<name>Stacy Keltner, Chair of the Department of Interdisciplinary Studies and Professor of Philosophy, Kennesaw State University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/stacy-keltner-336357"/>
paras: When Anne Carson learned she had won the Nobel Prize in literature, she was in Iceland, where, according to the Swedish Academy , she was “listening to the wind.”
Carson didn’t answer her phone right away, silencing it until her husband persuaded her to call back . Her verdict on the academy’s choice: “I think you’re all insane.”
Whatever she felt in the moment, there is an irony in Carson’s Nobel win. The highest award in literature has gone to a writer who has spent her career exploring the emptiness of a desire fulfilled.
The honor coincides with the 40th anniversary of the publication of her first book, “ Eros the Bittersweet ,” a meditation on desire.

In it, Carson argues that desire begins with a void – with wanting what we don’t have. She traces how this feeling of absence shapes love, reading, writing and thinking, activities that renew themselves precisely because they are never complete.

“Eros” begins with a brief preface on Franz Kafka’s “ The Top ,” a story about a philosopher who spends his time around children so he can chase their spinning tops. When a child sets a top in motion, the philosopher snatches it, believing that understanding any small thing, even a spinning top, would be enough to understand everything.
While the top spins, the philosopher is filled with hope, but as soon as he grasps it, he is repelled by the dumb piece of wood. He throws it down and waits for the next child to spin a top.

For Carson, the story is about why people love to fall in love. The philosopher is after what Carson calls an “impertinent stability in vertigo,” a state that is “itself delightful, a suspended moment of living hope.” The philosopher’s quest for knowledge, Carson cheekily concludes, is simply his pretext for chasing spinning tops. He is enchanted by the spinning itself, and even by his own enchantment – a spell that breaks the instant the top stops in his hand.

Most people know a version of this: There is something animating about chasing a goal. But once attained, the framed degree fades into the wall, the promotion quickly loses its luster, and the plaque becomes another dumb piece of wood.
The delight of wanting disappears in the having.
Why does fulfillment so often feel like loss?

Carson’s answer begins with the Greek word for erotic love, “eros,” which she explains denotes want or lack. Plato’s Socrates makes the same point in the “ Symposium .” For the Greeks, no one desires what they already have.

Desire also opens up an absence. To long for someone or something is to discover our own edges, the chasm where the self ends and what is wanted begins. Eros reveals that we are incomplete – an awareness that causes the self to become undone, loosening at the joints.
In one of her poems, the Greek poet Sappho called this experience “ glukupikron ,” or “sweetbitter.”
Carson’s translation of the passage reads : “Eros once again limb-loosener whirls me / sweetbitter, impossible to fight off, creature stealing up.”

Sappho puts sweet first, Carson notes in “Eros,” but desire is not initially sweet and then bitter. Pleasure and pain arrive together, in the same body and at the same time, before the lover is even able to distinguish them.

Carson extends this pattern to reading, writing and thinking. A reader approaches a text’s meaning but never masters it; every rereading turns up new meanings. The pleasure of understanding and the ache of incompleteness arrive together.

Writing works the same way. A good sentence both captures and conceals what the writer means. Thinking also runs on that doubled feeling, which is how the story of a philosopher chasing tops ended up in a book about love.
The same bittersweet pattern also shows up somewhere far less romantic: at work. Meeting a deadline brings relief that is already hollow because the next one is waiting.

I discovered “Eros the Bittersweet” as a philosophy graduate student, when my goals were to read, write and think my way into questions I loved. Now I spend much of my day as a university administrator, where the quality of my work is measured in metrics and met deadlines. Somewhere along the way, my goals stopped being things I wanted and became things to check off.

Today’s productivity culture chases tops of its own, but it looks less like Kafka’s philosopher than like Lucy and Ethel working at the chocolate factory in the 1952 “ I Love Lucy ” episode “ Job Switching .” As the conveyor belt speeds up, the only way they can look like they’re keeping up is to stuff what they’ve missed into their mouths.

Few things capture this pressure more than the SMART goal. In 1981, management consultant George Doran proposed that goals be SMART : specific, measurable, assignable, realistic and time-related. The acronym spread through industries and disciplines as a model for strategic planning, project management, performance evaluations and personal goal-setting. It distills a wider creed: Set the target, sprint after it, hit it. Grasp the top, toss it, capture the next one, ad infinitum. Doran didn’t invent the impulse, but his acronym gave it a checklist.
Carson’s account of desire helps explain why this creed leads to two kinds of emptiness.

The first comes from pursuing goals people never really desired. Inbox zero and a quarterly metric are goals in service of goals, the ultimate of which is productivity itself, which often simply ends up boosting someone else’s productivity.

The second comes from goals people truly wanted. Psychologist Tal Ben-Shahar calls the letdown that follows the “ arrival fallacy ” – the belief that reaching a destination will bring lasting happiness.

The Greeks offer another kind of striving, one that locates pleasure in the pursuit itself rather than in the prize. In Plato’s “ Phaedrus ,” Socrates describes eros as giving the soul wings and treats philosophy as a love of wisdom no one can own.

Centuries later, philosopher Alasdair MacIntyre distinguished external goods, such as money and status, from goods internal to a practice, such as a farmer’s growing mastery of her land or an architect’s pursuit of elegant, functional design. MacIntyre’s example, in his 1981 book “ After Virtue ,” is a child paid in candy to learn chess. As long as she plays for the candy, she has every reason to cheat. Only when she comes to love the game does she gain what chess itself can give: a particular kind of analytical skill, strategic imagination and competitive intensity.
To Socrates, MacIntyre and Carson, external goods get used up as they are won. Internal goods deepen the longer we pursue them.

Keeping desire alive means choosing pursuits that can never be finished – a craft, a field of study, a relationship – and letting the gap between reaching and grasping stay open. In this way, the lack that can hollow us out can also be what moves us.

Carson was handed the highest prize in literature. Yet the picture the Swedish Academy left us with is of a writer standing in the Icelandic wind, attending to a force of nature that no one can catch.
