articles.title: Florida Department of Health considers dropping 4 school vaccine requirements – here’s what that could mean for kids
articles.author:
<name>Katrine L. Wallace, Assistant Professor of Epidemiology and Biostatistics, University of Illinois Chicago</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/katrine-l-wallace-2626740"/>
paras: The Florida Department of Health held a hearing in October 2026 on a proposal to remove four vaccine requirements for entry into school and childcare: Haemophilus influenzae type b, or Hib , chickenpox , pneumococcal and hepatitis B .

These vaccines entered use in the U.S. at different times from the early 1980s through 2000. Prior to that, there were millions of chickenpox cases and thousands of serious bacterial infections and preventable deaths among American children each year. Vaccination has dramatically reduced the toll of these diseases.

Many parents today grew up during the transition to widespread vaccination for these diseases and may never have witnessed the severe complications these vaccines help prevent. I’m an epidemiologist who studies vaccine-preventable illnesses and health communication , and I worry that perhaps the luxury of forgetting about these diseases could end up giving rise to a generation of children who aren’t vaccinated against them.

School vaccination requirements help communities establish herd immunity , which is when enough people are vaccinated to prevent a disease from easily spreading. When vaccination rates fall, infections can spread among susceptible children throughout the community, placing those who are too young to be fully vaccinated, as well as those who cannot develop adequate protection due to medical conditions, at greater risk.

Florida’s proposal would not eliminate these four vaccines, nor would ending a mandate mean that every family would stop using them. However, it would weaken one of the policies designed to maintain high vaccination coverage. If fewer children are vaccinated as a result, the risks will extend beyond the families making that choice.

Before Hib vaccines became widely used in the late 1980s, pediatricians sometimes faced a terrifying emergency: an infant with fever, lethargy and a stiff neck. Testing of cerebrospinal fluid would reveal bacterial meningitis caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b, or Hib , an infection that could kill a child or leave lasting neurological damage.
Today, many doctors have never even seen a single case. The bacterium has not disappeared, but widespread vaccination has made serious Hib disease in young children far less common.

Before the vaccine, Hib was the leading cause of bacterial meningitis . In the early 1980s, there were 20,000 invasive Hib infections among American children under 5 years old, 12,000 of which were meningitis. Between 3% and 6% of those children died , and between 15% and 30% of the survivors were left deaf or with brain damage.
Hib infection did not manifest in dramatic outbreaks. Healthy young children carried it silently, and some, unpredictably, became seriously ill.

After the introduction of conjugate vaccines for Hib in the late 1980s, cases among young children declined by 99% . In 2023, the United States reported only 13 cases in children under 5 . In 2026, that number is up to 28 .

By the early 1990s, there were more than 4 million cases of chickenpox annually in the United States. Of those infected, 10,500 to 13,500 were hospitalized, and 100 to 150 died. More than 90% of cases and about 70% of hospitalizations occurred in children, as did roughly half of the deaths.
But even those who had manageable cases of childhood chickenpox are at risk for shingles later in life, which can lead to painful and sometimes permanent health complications .

Children are contagious before the rash appears, and each case has an incubation period of up to three weeks . A single infection could spread through a school or daycare in waves for a month or more. Since vaccination began in 1995, deaths from chickenpox in people under 20 years old have been virtually eliminated .
Pneumococcal bacteria can live harmlessly in a child’s upper respiratory tract – that is, the nose – but if it moves into the blood or organs, it can cause serious damage.

Before the introduction of the childhood vaccine in 2000, pneumococcal disease caused about 17,000 invasive infections annually in American children under 5 years old, including about 700 cases of meningitis and 200 deaths . On top of that, pneumococcal disease caused approximately 5 million ear infections.

Hepatitis B can spread from an infected mother to her baby during childbirth and through contact with infected blood. People with chronic hepatitis B may have no symptoms and may not know they are infected, allowing the virus to spread unknowingly within families and communities. Infected infants and young children also are often asymptomatic.

Yet the consequences can be serious. Infants who become infected with hepatitis B have about a 90% chance of developing chronic hepatitis B , which over time can cause cirrhosis and liver cancer. The risk of chronic infection falls sharply with age, making prevention of infection early in life particularly important.
Before the hepatitis B vaccine became available in the U.S. in 1982, an estimated 20,000 American children were infected each year.

In 1991, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommended universal infant hepatitis B vaccination as part of a comprehensive strategy to prevent transmission. The CDC estimates that perinatal hepatitis B infections in the United States declined by 75% between 1987 and 2000.

Florida’s historical records for these diseases are incomplete. For example, chickenpox was not a disease tracked by the Florida Department of Health until late 2006 . That makes it difficult to reconstruct the state’s prevaccine impact of these diseases from surveillance records alone.

But Florida doesn’t have to imagine what happens when vaccination is neglected: Measles has resurfaced in the state this year. It had previously been eliminated nationally in 2000 , meaning sustained endemic transmission had been interrupted. The disease has never been eradicated globally, and imported infections can trigger outbreaks when they reach undervaccinated communities.

An outbreak at Ave Maria University outside of Naples infected at least 62 people , and the state reported 162 cases as of Oct. 17, 2026. This is the most recent available data at the time of this article’s publication.

The proposal to stop requiring vaccines for hepatitis B, chickenpox, Hib and pneumococcal comes as only 88.9% of Florida kindergartners received the measles, mumps, rubella – or MMR – vaccine during the 2025-26 school year. This is below both the U.S. national average of 92.4% and the recommended threshold of 95% to create herd immunity.

Unfortunately, it’s been difficult to know current measles rates in Florida. In May 2026, the Florida Department of Health removed county-level disease data from its website. The data has since been replaced, but there is currently no measles dashboard to track cases in the state. The department’s 2026 counts have often been delayed , and public tracking systems disagree on the statewide total.

An entire generation of parents has been spared the experience of seeing a child with Hib meningitis, or young adults with liver problems from chronic hepatitis B. Nor have they had to deal with finding alternate childcare for a month because a chickenpox outbreak has shut down their child’s preschool. These are achievements of vaccination – and a reminder of what can be forgotten when prevention works.

articles.title: Figuring out where cosmic neutrinos come from is tricky - radio telescopes could help find where these ‘ghost particles’ originate
articles.author:
<name>Yjan Gordon, Instructor of Physics, University of Wisconsin-Whitewater</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/yjan-gordon-2691193"/>
paras: Neutrinos are funny little particles that weigh almost nothing, making them one of the universe’s most elusive building blocks. They can come from objects as mundane as bananas and as exotic as supernovas – the exploding death throes of massive stars. Most neutrinos stream through space and pass through the Earth without interacting with anything.

An experiment called IceCube, built to detect these “ghost particles” emitted from astrophysical events, just won a Nobel Prize . As a physicist , I’m interested in figuring out where the neutrinos IceCube detects come from. A study that my colleagues and I published in October 2026 suggests that we could potentially use radio telescopes to answer this question.

Even though these telescopes can’t see neutrinos, we can use their data to match up IceCube’s detections with their potential sources out in space. Knowing which types of objects produce neutrinos can tell astronomers about the physics occurring within those objects.

Most particles interact with the universe through a fundamental force of nature called electromagnetism . It’s the force that powers the phone, tablet or computer that you may be reading this article on. It drives all the chemistry responsible for life, and it’s responsible for the light your eyes can see.

What makes neutrinos odd is that they don’t interact with the universe through electromagnetism. Instead, they interact with the universe via a force that physicists call the weak interaction . This force only acts over distances smaller than the inside of an atomic nucleus ; as such, they must pass very, very close to the centers of atoms in order to interact – otherwise they just fly right through. That makes them very difficult to detect – but not impossible.
Scientists have been able to detect neutrinos from space – called astrophysical neutrinos – since the 1960s. These typically come from our Sun and, in at least one case, from a supernova .

Over the past decade or so, researchers at the appropriately named IceCube Observatory have used the South Pole’s Antarctic ice as a neutrino telescope. The densely packed ice gives neutrinos many opportunities to interact with water molecules, and detectors can see radiation from those interactions when they do occur.

Even so, neutrinos really are one of nature’s most introverted particles, and it takes time for any of the ice molecules to get lucky and interact with a neutrino. But, with enough time, it eventually happens. And with more time, it happens again. The more time you give it, the more interactions you see, and the more neutrinos you detect.

IceCube has used this approach to detect astrophysical neutrinos that are hundreds of thousands of times more energetic than those previously seen. The discovery of these high-energy astrophysical neutrinos has opened up a new window on our universe.

The same property that makes them difficult to detect – namely their reluctance to interact with their surroundings – also makes them an effective way to see high-energy processes in places that light can’t penetrate. The problem is we’re not sure where they all come from.

Scientists do have some ideas about their origin, of course. Quasars – objects where matter is being ripped apart by black holes millions of times more massive than our Sun – seem to be likely candidates. In 2017, IceCube detected a neutrino that appeared to come from the direction of a quasar , known as TXS 0506+056, at the same time that a telescope detected an outburst of gamma radiation from that same object.

That finding is interesting because the processes that produce neutrinos – namely the decay of subatomic particles – should also produce high-energy electromagnetic radiation – namely gamma rays. So scientists expect neutrino sources to also produce gamma-ray outbursts.

However, TXS 0506+056 is just one object. It may not be representative of where most high-energy neutrinos come from. So far, there’s been little evidence of a more general relationship between gamma-ray outbursts and neutrino detections. But gamma rays can be easily obscured.

Much like the lead apron that the technician taking your X-ray at the hospital wears to protect themselves from the radiation, dust and gas that gathers near a supermassive black hole can block gamma rays from ever reaching Earth.

However, another form of electromagnetic radiation that’s invisible to gamma-ray telescopes – radio waves – are not so easily shielded. Using telescopes that look at radio waves from space may provide scientists an alternate way to see what’s going on.

Beginning in 2017, the Very Large Array in New Mexico began tracking how radio emissions from space change in brightness over time, a project known as the Very Large Array Sky Survey , or VLASS for short. My team and I recently showed that most of the objects seen by VLASS with fluctuating radio emissions are quasars , of the same type that IceCube previously saw producing neutrinos.
Interestingly, when we compared the times that IceCube detected neutrinos with the times when objects spotted by VLASS experienced flares of radio emission, there appeared to be a correlation.

Put another way, when an astrophysical neutrino is detected by IceCube, there is a radio source brightening in the same part of the sky, more often than you’d expect from random chance . These radio flares seem to only be associated with about 13% of the astrophysical neutrinos detected by IceCube, which means we still can’t account for the origin of the majority of astrophysical neutrinos. However, more than 90% of the radio outbursts potentially associated with neutrinos aren’t seen at all by our gamma-ray telescopes.
If the neutrino’s source of origin is hidden at gamma-ray wavelengths, but not at radio wavelengths, then radio telescopes could become an essential tool in neutrino astronomy.

At the moment, the signal we’re seeing is intriguing, even tantalizing. But there’s about a 1-in-30 chance of getting the results we see even if there’s no correlation between neutrinos and radio flares. Those are roughly the same odds as tossing a coin five times and getting heads every time: unlikely, but not impossible.

Scientists are far more comfortable when the odds of a result being due to random chance are closer to one in a million – the same as getting heads 20 times in a row. To confirm if what we’re seeing is real or not, we need more observations. We expect to have those in the next few years.
One thing is for sure, though: It’s an exciting time to be studying the origins of astrophysical neutrinos, and it looks like radio astronomers may have a big role to play.

articles.title: How moving civil rights enforcement out of the US Department of Education threatens students’ protections from race, sex and disability discrimination
articles.author:
<name>Bridget Joyce, Director of Programming at Education Rights Institute, University of Virginia</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/bridget-joyce-2741021"/>
paras: Many people are not familiar with the Office for Civil Rights , an office within the U.S. Department of Education that enforces statutes that protect students from discrimination. So, it might help to consider a recent example of this office’s work.

In December 2022, the Office for Civil Rights, or OCR, found that Ottumwa Community School District, about 90 miles southeast of Des Moines, Iowa, had violated Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 by failing to address racial harassment. Title VI bars schools receiving federal funds from discriminating based on race, color or national origin.

The harassment was so severe that the office found that the student “was subjected to a racially hostile environment.” OCR also found that the school and district “failed to address the pervasive racial harassment of which it was aware.”

The harassment spanned two school years, during which that student was called “blackie,” “slave,” “cotton picker” and other racial slurs. One white student knelt on a Gatorade bottle and said, “It can’t breathe,” mocking the murder of George Floyd, according to the complaint.

Ottumwa Community School District entered a resolution agreement with OCR and agreed to reimburse the student’s family for therapy . The district also agreed to train students and staff on nondiscrimination policies, among other actions .

We spent a combined 17 years at the U.S. Department of Education – one of us in the Office of the General Counsel from 1999 to 2004 and the other in OCR from 2013 to 2025. We saw firsthand the pivotal role that OCR plays in protecting students’ civil rights.

In June 2026, the Trump administration announced a new interagency agreement that provides a way to shift OCR’s day-to-day civil rights enforcement responsibilities from the Department of Education to the Department of Justice .

The administration has not released details on whether OCR has begun to transfer enforcement responsibilities to the Department of Justice under the June 2026 interagency agreement or what, exactly, that would look like.
But this reorganization may mean that most complaints filed with OCR will never be investigated, and those that are could take years to resolve.
In fiscal year 2024 – October 2023 through September 2024 – OCR received over 22,000 complaints related to discrimination based on race, color, national origin, sex and disability.

Individuals and families who file complaints with OCR may want to avoid the expense of filing a lawsuit in a federal court or to secure relief for a student more quickly than a federal court can provide it.

OCR typically seeks to resolve any violations of the laws that it enforces through voluntary resolution agreements, initiating proceedings to terminate federal funding to school districts only when voluntary resolution is not possible, which has historically been rare.
The Department of Education and Department of Justice announced in June 2026 that they had entered an interagency agreement to “ deepen their partnership to secure equal access to education .”
Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights Harmeet Dhillon explained that the Department of Justice would handle OCR’s complaints “from soup to nuts,” taking on “99 percent” of that work.
This is another step toward the Trump administration’s 2025 promise to close the Department of Education, though only Congress can do that .
Moving the Office for Civil Rights’ enforcement responsibilities to the Department of Justice will significantly change how Title VI and other federal civil rights laws are enforced in schools.

The Department of Justice’s Educational Opportunities Section has long jointly enforced most of the laws that OCR enforces, with each agency generally separately handling its own cases under these laws.
However, there are a few important distinctions between how OCR and the Department of Justice enforce civil rights laws.

First, the Office for Civil Rights is legally required to consider every complaint that it receives. It also must promptly investigate complaints that show possible violations of federal civil rights laws.

A January 2026 Government and Accountability Office report found that OCR dismissed about 90% of complaints for part of 2025, raising questions about whether OCR was dismissing complaints without full review during that time. Historically, however, we have seen OCR comply with the requirement to consider all complaints.

In contrast, the Department of Justice’s Educational Opportunities Section selects only a small fraction of cases to pursue, usually tackling systemic or particularly severe discrimination in federal courts.
Both agencies carry out important civil rights work.

But shifting OCR’s enforcement responsibilities to the Department of Justice will mean that students lose their guarantee that a federal agency will review and evaluate their allegations that a school district violated their civil rights.
Another distinction is that the Office for Civil Rights typically resolves complaints on its own, without involving federal courts.
OCR has traditionally aimed to resolve complaints within 180 days of receipt , because unresolved discrimination hinders students’ ability to learn.
It can sometimes take longer than this to reach a resolution. Between October 2023 and September 2024, for example, OCR did not resolve approximately 30% of the complaints received within 180 days.
In contrast, the Department of Justice’s Educational Opportunities Section can sometimes take years to resolve its cases in court.
A third distinction is that the Department of Justice’s Educational Opportunities Section is not staffed to handle the volume of civil rights complaints that the Office for Civil Rights receives.
From October 2023 through September 2024, OCR received a record high of 22,687 complaints and employed just under 600 full-time equivalent employees.
OCR investigations and resolutions were still backlogged during the early 2020s.
The number of complaints filed with OCR climbed even higher between October 2024 and September 2025 .
The Department of Education reported there were 446 staff employed at OCR in November 2025.

In contrast, the Department of Justice’s Educational Opportunities Section employed about 40 lawyers in January 2025 and had lost the majority of its staff by June 2025. The Educational Opportunities Section has not published a more recent estimate of its staffing.
Even before the Trump administration, OCR was held back by inadequate funding.
The number of civil rights complaints submitted to OCR has skyrocketed over the past decade, but staffing has not kept pace.
In the early 1980s there was about one staff member for every three new complaints filed at OCR.
By 2024 that ratio had increased to one staff member for every 39 new complaints filed .
During the Biden administration, Congress denied repeated requests from the White House to increase funding to OCR .

Since January 2025, the administration has closed seven of OCR’s 12 regional offices . The administration also tried to lay off approximately half of OCR’s workforce in March 2025, with additional layoffs in October, but withdrew those layoffs following successful legal challenges.
OCR reached resolution agreements in less than 1% of pending cases in 2025, down from 5% in 2024, according to findings from a U.S. Senate committee report chaired by Sen. Bernie Sanders.

articles.title: Tech Moves: Former Amazon execs depart Warner Bros. Discovery; Amazon leader returns to Microsoft
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: — Two former Amazon executives who helped build Discovery ’s direct-to-consumer operation in Bellevue, Wash., are stepping down from their leadership roles following the company’s acquisition by Paramount Skydance. They will remain in advisory roles during the transition.

Avi Saxena joined Discovery in 2019 as chief technology officer of its direct-to-consumer business and led its new Bellevue office. He became CTO of Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD) following Discovery’s 2022 merger with AT&T’s WarnerMedia business. Paramount Skydance completed its acquisition of WBD on Oct. 6, with the combined company taking the name Skydance Corporation.

Before joining Discovery, Saxena was with Amazon for 19 years over two stints, most recently as vice president of technology for Amazon Marketplace. He also held leadership roles at Microsoft and internet infrastructure startups.

Tyler Whitworth is stepping down as executive vice president and chief product officer for WBD’s streaming business. He led teams working on digital products for HBO Max, discovery+, Eurosport, TNT Sports, Food Network and others. Before joining Discovery, he spent more than seven years at Amazon, leading teams developing products and services for customers and third-party sellers.
Dane Glasgow, Skydance’s chief product officer, announced the departures of Whitworth, Saxena and WBD Chief Information Officer Dave Duvall in a memo shared with GeekWire.
“Much of the strength of WBD’s product and technology organizations reflects their leadership and dedication. Please join me in thanking them and wishing them the very best,” Glasgow wrote.
The company has not responded to GeekWire’s inquiries about the future of the Bellevue office.

— Bahadir Onalan is returning to Microsoft as a vice president in its CoreAI organization, focused on responsible AI, after nearly 10 years at Amazon. Onalan first joined Microsoft in 2005 and worked on Azure teams focused on search, analytics, business intelligence and security. He left in 2017 as a principal software group engineering manager to join Amazon, where he worked on machine learning initiatives.
“This second tenure feels like a true homecoming,” Onalan wrote . “Our goal goes beyond shipping a platform or a product; we are here to define the global standards for AI safety.”

— Naria Santa Lucia is leaving Microsoft after seven years, most recently as a general manager with Microsoft Elevate. She previously served as executive director of the Washington State Opportunity Scholarship.

“I’ll carry the lessons I learned from my time at Microsoft as I continue my personal and professional mission to serve people and communities by teaching, advising nonprofits and mission driven organizations, and spreading joy and human connection,” Santa Lucia wrote .
She did not announce a specific next role.

— VertueLab , a Pacific Northwest nonprofit supporting climate tech entrepreneurs, has named Leo Ochoa executive director, promoting him from managing director for Oregon. He succeeds Aina Abiodun , who is transitioning to chair of the organization’s board after more than three years as executive director.

“Leo brings a unique blend of vision, relationships, and entrepreneurship experience,” the organization said , noting his background as a wildland firefighter, startup founder and patent holder for wearable safety gear.
Abiodun’s accomplishments include co-creating the Seattle Climate Innovation Hub, launching the Opalene Climate Challenge and helping lead the Just Future Climate Labs initiative.

— Seattle’s Pulse Space has appointed Leah Sardone as vice president of engineering. The startup is developing laser-based systems to deliver power and enable long-distance communications in low Earth orbit and beyond. In July, the company announced a $40 million U.S. Space Force contract to advance its laser-based space power technology.

Sardone brings more than 23 years of experience in hardware, sensors and embedded systems development. She joins Pulse Space from IonQ, where she most recently served as director of quantum networking and interconnects. Her previous employers include Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, Honeywell Aerospace, Blue Origin and Amazon’s Project Kuiper, now known as Amazon Leo.

— Caravel Bio a Portland, Ore., startup developing technology to rapidly test newly designed proteins, has announced Michał Jastrzębski as its CTO. The company says its platform can screen millions of protein designs in parallel at low cost, helping identify promising candidates for applications in human health, pollution reduction and industrial processes.
Caravel also announced a nearly $1.25 million Small Business Innovation Research Phase II grant from the National Science Foundation to further develop the platform.
Jastrzębski previously served as a principal machine learning engineer at Ginkgo Bioworks. His past employers also include GitHub and Intel.

— Darick Baker has been appointed the director the University of Washington’s Washington Nanofabrication Facility , which the UW describes as “the largest publicly accessible nanofabrication facility and cleanroom in the Pacific Northwest.” Baker joined the facility in 2012 as a research engineer and has served as acting director since 2025. He previously worked at the Colorado School of Mines
— Technology Alliance announced that Stoke Space director of communications Kyra Jorgensen has joined its board. Jorgeson recently joined the space startup from the fusion company Helion Energy.

articles.title: AWS growth hits 39%, its fastest in nearly five years, as Amazon misses on earnings
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Amazon Web Services revenue grew 39% to $46 billion in the third quarter , its fastest pace in nearly five years, and Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said he expects the cloud unit to top 40% growth in both 2027 and 2028.

That wasn’t enough for investors. Amazon posted earnings of $1.89 per share, well short of the $1.97 analysts expected, as higher interest costs on its growing debt and other losses ate into its profit.
Operating income beat expectations at $28.1 billion, above the high end of Amazon’s own guidance, and the 13.9% operating margin for the quarter was the highest in the company’s history.

Revenue of $201.9 billion, up 12%, came in just under analyst estimates but at the top of Amazon’s forecast range. Shares fell more than 7% in after-hours trading, after closing down 4% during the regular session.

Update: On the earnings call, Jassy said AWS has a backlog of $578 billion in contracted future revenue, more than double a year earlier. He also said Amazon expects to spend “meaningfully more” on capital projects in 2027 than the roughly $220 billion it plans for this year.
Amazon may need to count on its legendary willingness to be “misunderstood for long periods of time,” as it asks investors to look past the costs to where its biggest businesses are headed.

In the company’s earnings release , Jassy said Amazon’s retail business is gaining market share with improving margins. Retail sales, including online stores, physical stores and third-party seller services, totaled nearly $500 billion over the past 12 months, and AWS is now at a $184 billion annual revenue run rate.
“There has never been a trillion dollar revenue business, and we may have two of them in the next 5-10 years,” he said.
On the earnings call, Jassy said those two businesses are AWS and Amazon’s stores business.

Advertising grew 11% to $19.6 billion, or 12% excluding currency changes, down from 22% on that basis a year earlier. Amazon blamed the timing of Prime Day and a few other factors, and said it expects ad growth to return to the high teens in the fourth quarter.

Online stores grew 2% to $68.5 billion, held back by Prime Day moving into the second quarter this year. Amazon said overall revenue growth would have been about 4 percentage points higher without the shift.
Third-party seller services , the fees Amazon collects from merchants on its site, grew 9% to $46.5 billion. AWS came within about $500 million of it.
Subscription services , which includes Prime memberships, grew 11% to $14 billion.
Physical stores , mostly Whole Foods, grew 2% to $5.7 billion.
Outlook: Amazon expects fourth-quarter revenue of $240 billion to $247 billion, up 12% to 16%, and operating income of $28.5 billion to $33.5 billion.

Amazon CFO Brian Olsavsky said on the earnings call that costs for Amazon Leo, the company’s satellite internet service, are weighing on its fourth-quarter profit forecast as the service gets ready to launch later this year.

Wall Street had expected fourth-quarter operating income of $33.2 billion, near the top of that range, according to analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives. It still expects to spend about $220 billion on capital projects this year.

Amazon’s free cash flow, the cash left over after capital spending, was negative $42.4 billion over the past 12 months, compared with positive $14.8 billion a year earlier, mostly because of its AI investments.

articles.title: Sound Transit Pilots Updated Pet Policy
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: Sound Transit is piloting an updated pet policy on its buses and trains between now and Spring 2027. During the pilot, pet dogs will be permitted on board if they are leashed, well-behaved, and controlled by their handler. All other pets must remain in an enclosed carrier. As always, service animals are permitted in compliance with the ADA.

Prior to the pilot, dogs and other pets were only allowed on Sound Transit buses and trains in a carrier. In July 2025, the Sound Transit Board approved Motion No. M2025-34 , directing the agency to consider updating the rules to allow leashed dogs. This motion was motivated by the opening of Marymoor Village station as part of the Downtown Redmond Link Extension in May 2025. Marymoor Village station is next to Marymoor Park, a 640-arce park which includes a 40-arce off-leash dog area.

Will this pilot impact the passenger experience on Sound Transit? Probably not. In a presentation to the Executive Committee before the motion was approved, then-Acting Executive Director of Security & Fare Engagement Brian de Place acknowledged that passengers already take leashed dogs on Sound Transit buses and trains. While doing so did violate the rules, de Place noted “if the dog is leashed and generally under control, security will not engage with that passenger unless there is an actual disturbance”. In the year prior to this meeting, Sound Transit security only received 8 calls about pets.
There are few other notes pet owners should be aware of before bringing their leashed dogs onboard:
If you encounter an aggressive animal or other issues, call or text Sound Transit security: (206) 398-5268. In an emergency, call 911.

articles.title: Seattle Opens Its Largest Tiny House Village Yet in South Park
articles.author: Amy Sundberg
paras: On Tuesday, the Low Income Housing Institute (LIHI) celebrated the opening of its new Cloverleaf Tiny House Village, its largest tiny house village to date. Located in an industrial neighborhood in South Park right off Highway 99, the new tiny house village has 90 tiny houses measuring in at 8 by 12 feet and will be able to house approximately 100 people.

“When I look around, I think this is what progress looks like,” Wilson said at the grand opening. “This is 90 tiny houses, 90 doors that lock, 90 chances for someone to come inside and catch their breath and find a new beginning. And of course, Cloverleaf Village is also a part of something bigger, a commitment that we as a city are finally ready to keep.”

Wilson was referring to Seattle’s long struggle with unsheltered homelessness, which led Mayor Ed Murray to declare a state of emergency on homelessness in 2015. More than a decade later, the problem persists. The 2026 Point in Time Count in King County, conducted by the King County Regional Homelessness Authority, recorded a 9% increase in the number of unhoused people since 2024’s count, with a larger percentage of those people being unsheltered.

Plus, service providers are bracing as federal policy changes , including at the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development and through cuts to health insurance subsidies, Apple Health, and SNAP , risk increasing that number further. Decisions from the Trump administration are weakening the social safety net, leaving more at risk of homelessness.

This new tiny house village is a product of Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson’s shelter accelerator plan and was funded by a public-private partnership with Challenge Seattle with support from the Seattle Foundation. The City of Seattle will continue to support the village’s operating costs in the future, assuming that the Seattle City Council passes that section of Wilson’s proposed 2027 budget as is.

“The mayor told us that addressing chronic homelessness was among her highest priorities,” said Christine Gregoire, former governor and CEO of Challenge Seattle. “We asked how the business community could be of help to her, and today we're here because our members stepped forward with $3 million to help make that priority a real reality. For years, Challenge Seattle has advocated for stronger, comprehensive, better coordinated public-private partners to address chronic homelessness. This is the vision that we've always had.”

Cloverleaf’s church sponsor is Reverend Lawrence Willis with the New Direction Missionary Baptist Church. Having a church sponsor expedites the process of standing up a new tiny house village, and the sponsor will often participate in a village’s community advisory committee.

Tyson, otherwise known as Turtle, a former resident of LIHI’s tiny house village Camp Second Chance, also spoke at the opening. Since his time at Camp Second Chance, he’s moved into his own apartment.

“Your support didn't just build tiny houses,” Tyson told the crowd. “You built a figurative scaffold that we all will be able to use to then build our own futures. With a safe place for people to land, they won't be so hesitant to test their wings and fly.”

In addition to the housing units, the village features a large kitchen tent, 10 bathroom stalls with toilet, sink, and shower, both outdoor and indoor community spaces, and a laundry room. The laundry machines will be free to use with soap provided, and residents of the village will be fed three meals a day by Operation Sack Lunch.

Both case management and behavioral health services will be provided on site. In the past, Sharon Lee, the executive director of LIHI, said their tiny house villages couldn’t afford to provide behavioral health services on site as part of their wrap-around services.

This particular village will be for adults only and will allow pets, with a dog run in the back and available dog waste bag dispensers. Some units have a double bed in order to be suitable for couples, and 12 of the units are ADA compliant. Each unit is also equipped with air conditioning and a space heater.
Security cameras are spaced at regular intervals throughout the village and monitored on-site. Staff will be present on site 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

The village is a bit of a trek from public transit – the nearest bus stop is more than half a mile away – with some of the surrounding streets lacking sidewalks. Those same streets handle significant truck traffic due to the businesses located there. LIHI plans to run a shuttle to help with accessibility, but the shuttle’s frequency and hours have not yet been determined.

“We are currently working to finalize the transportation plan for Cloverleaf,” LIHI senior manager of communications and resource development Alexis Diltz told The Urbanist . “We anticipate purchasing a shuttle van soon and will be developing the schedule and routes as we move forward with implementation. We want to ensure the transportation plan reflects program participants’ needs and priorities, so participant feedback and input will be an important part of that process.”
Diltz added that the shuttle will be providing transport to nearby grocery stores.

Soon after she assumed office, Wilson took steps to expedite the creation of new shelter spaces, including transmitting three pieces of legislation to the city council: one identifying additional spending for emergency shelter in 2026, one giving the city authority to sign leases for larger pieces of land at market rates, and one increasing the baseline and maximum number of people accepted at shelter sites.
All three ultimately passed , although not without friction between the council and the Mayor’s Office.

“When I stepped into office, it was my very highest priority to figure out how we could build a lot more shelter fast, and not just a roof over people's heads, but shelter that comes with services, the services that many people living unsheltered on our streets need in order to find that new beginning,” Wilson said.
Since her term began, Wilson has overseen the opening of Bayside Shelter in Interbay and Brighton Village in Rainier Valley.
Sharon Lee, the executive director of LIHI, credited Wilson with helping to expedite the opening of Cloverleaf.

“[Wilson] got every department head to get together in one room and look at our plans and permits and said, "Hey, anybody has any issues with this? You need to speak up now, and we're going to approve the permits. That had never happened before,” Lee told The Urbanist . “For a tiny house village, it was almost like the shortest period of time ever to get a permit.”
Lee said that without Wilson’s extra push, Cloverleaf wouldn’t have been able to open until next year.
Donna Anderson, the regional operations manager for LIHI, shared the crucial role that living in a tiny house village played in her ability to overcome addiction and take the next steps in her life.

“I want to thank the mayor. This is the first time in a very long time that I've had hope that we can actually make things better, and there is one outstanding reason why,” Anderson said. “For a very long time, the administrations have not been listening to the folks who are doing the work on the ground, to us who are out here doing the work every day. And this administration is listening. They're listening to nonprofits, they're listening to what works and what doesn't work. So we're not just throwing money at something that's not going to work. We're evolving. We're funding more services. We're funding the services that are needed.”

Last week, Wilson announced a new neighborhood-centered strategy to allocate the new shelter spaces the City is opening as effectively as possible. The new spots available at Cloverleaf will be key for executing that strategy, and on-site behavioral health specialists will mean the village can provide essential services for higher acuity residents.

Glassyards Commons, also being run by LIHI, is scheduled to open in November , providing parking for 72 recreational vehicles (RVs) and 20 tiny houses, which Lee said will serve upwards of 140 people because “just about every RV has more than one person.”

The reality that most RVs house multiple people calls into question Seattle Councilmember Dan Strauss’s new RV permitting program , which would only allow an individual person who could prove themselves to be the registered owner of an RV to receive a permit.
Early next year, LIHI is also scheduled to open a seven-story building on 125th and Aurora with 90 apartments for seniors aged 62 and above making up to 50% of the area median income.
Also on the schedule for the City is a Purpose Dignity Action (PDA) operated shelter and expansions at three existing shelters.

With Cloverleaf open and Glassyards Commons scheduled to open soon, the South Park neighborhood will be the location of three homeless shelters, with Camp Second Chance located there as well. KIRO 7 reported that Camp Second Chance is the leading candidate to expand to 250 units from its current 69, taking advantage of Wilson’s new legislation.
The Mayor’s Office didn’t respond to The Urbanist ’s inquiry about the factors it considers in its homeless shelter siting decisions.

“Shelters like Cloverleaf are really how we welcome people indoors, how we can stop this pattern of just moving people from block to block, how we can actually get people what they need in order to start over, and this is also how we overcome the cynicism that takes root when people lose the faith that we can actually solve our our greatest challenges together,” Wilson said. “What this is going to take is partnerships and persistence. And what gives me hope is not just seeing the tangible signs of progress here behind me, these actual tiny homes that people are already moving into, but knowing that those partnerships are strong, and knowing that we are all feeling very persistent right now.”

articles.title: New Harborview Garage Advances In Face of Soaring Hospital Expansion Costs
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: King County is advancing plans for a new, six-story underground parking garage adjacent to Harborview Medical Center. The parking project will put the first shovels in the ground on the major hospital expansion approved by voters in 2020. The $189 million garage is needed, county officials say, to mitigate the loss of hundreds of parking stalls when construction on a new Harborview medical tower begins next year, an inpatient facility that will add critical capacity to the strained hospital campus.

The garage's pending construction, set to commence next year, comes as costs on the overall Harborview bond program continue to escalate, going from $1.74 billion when it was approved six years ago to more than $3 billion today . That recent cost update, provided Tuesday morning to members of the King County Council by Harborview Construction and Infrastructure Division Director Tony Wright, is hundreds of millions of dollars more than had been communicated just a few months ago .

The parking garage is set to be constructed on what's currently a vacant lot at Ninth Avenue and Alder Street, which the County acquired in 2024. The project is advancing through permitting as a two-stage development that would see a multistory medical office building built sometime after the parking-only phase. But no funding has been identified for that second stage of the development, a project that falls outside of the core scope of the Harborview bond program.

The garage's total number of stalls – somewhere between 700 and 730 – stems from the site's zoning, which sits within the larger Yesler Terrace master-planned community (MPC). The total number of parking stalls within the boundaries of that MPC is capped at 1,350, with 749 stalls currently available after recent residential developments have opened in recent years.

King County did consider building a fully standalone parking garage on the site, but a recent report looking at parking alternatives notes that this is "likely not an allowable use" within the Yesler Terrace MPC.

When the new medical tower opens as soon as 2032, with approximately three stories of underground parking of its own, the net amount of off-street parking within the total Harborview campus will have increased by 550 stalls compared to today. If the medical office building is ultimately built at Ninth and Alder, some stalls would be lost due to a need to create a loading dock.

Harborview is the only Level 1 trauma center across a four-state area that includes Alaska, Montana, and Idaho, making expanding its inpatient capacity a pressing issue of regional significance. But it's not clear that Harborview has in fact utilized all of the tools in the toolbox to be able to enable patient and staff access without more vehicle parking.

During Tuesday's discussion, King County Councilmember Claudia Balducci pressed Wright on the decision to lead with construction on a parking garage, given the fact that the timeline to open the new medical tower has already slipped by four years. That new tower, in addition to providing badly needed inpatient beds, would also "provide surge capacity for the hospital to effectively respond to a disaster or mass casualty event," according to a recent program update .

"I would just love [it] if we were not breaking ground on a parking garage and spending all our time and money on a parking garage first," Balducci said. "I would rather we would get right into building the tower, which we so desperately need, and I just I hear everybody say in a very confident way, based on their personal experience and anecdotal observations, we need the parking. We cannot live without the parking. I have not seen an analysis of any attempts to come up with temporary parking that would have enabled us to go forward with the tower instead of spending yet more time and money on a parking garage first."

Even though the total number of stalls planned at Ninth and Alder stems from Yesler Terrace's zoning stipulations and not the Harborview’s Major Institution Master Plan (MIMP), Harborview CEO Sommer Kleweno Walley pointed to an internal demand study that spells out the need for the added garage space.

"There was a very large study done on demand, and what we're differentiating is the demand needed for patients to come to the campus for clinics and for visitors to come to the hospital versus staff," Kleweno Walley said. "So what we have done is pulled out how much parking we will need to accommodate clinics being on campus, visitors coming for the certain number of inpatient beds we have, and then certain types of staff, i.e., the providers who need to be there 24/7, where you can't ship them in, you can't wait for them to be brought in from a shuttle. So that is the demand we're looking at."

Steffanie Fain, who served on the Harborview board of trustees before joining the county council, also weighed in on the history that has caused the county to arrive at a garage-forward construction plan.

"There were a few ideas when this came forward as an option [of] what to do with that space, and it was: do we build a temporary parking structure to get us through construction and then figure out what to do with it? But it seems wild to spend millions of dollars on something that you just tear down," Fain said. "The medical office building is the next best sustainable option and could really be utilized in the future. Ideally, it would have been a medical surge space, but that was so extraordinarily expensive that that option quickly went away."

While the new garage isn't expected to be complete until late 2028, construction on the new medical tower is scheduled to start before it wraps up. Other related projects, including the construction of temporary roadways and entrances in order to allow work to proceed while hospital operations are maintained, are also expected to begin next year.

articles.title: Ten years of coffee, cuts, and causes: Squirrel Chops marks a decade at 23rd and Union
articles.author: AGPhoto
paras: When CHS first stopped by Squirrel Chops in 2016, Shirley Henderson told us she and partner Sharon Blyth-Moss wanted to make community building their business instead of their hobby. Ten years later, the coffee shop and two-chair salon just west of 23rd and Union is still pouring, still cutting, and still organizing.
“I honestly think it exceeded my expectations,” Henderson said.

Henderson, a longtime activist who was part of the “Fight for 15” campaign alongside Kshama Sawant , admits she was nervous early on about being openly political as a business owner. Squirrel Chops went on to back Tax Amazon, the 2020 protests against police violence, and Sawant’s runs for office. It turned out to be a draw.
“All of the things that we’ve stood for have only deepened people’s loyalty and respect for who we are as a business,” she said.

When Henderson wrote a Seattle Times op-ed during the Tax Amazon fight saying she paid more in taxes per dollar than Jeff Bezos, the shop got hate mail… and new regulars, including bus drivers who wanted to support a business willing to say so. Just this week, a customer said he came in because the shop supported Sawant’s congressional campaign .

To Henderson, owning a Central District business doesn’t conflict with her socialist politics. “We just happen to want to work for ourselves,” she said. “As a socialist, I want to treat staff with dignity and respect, because they are the backbone of this space.”

She is taking that platform to City Hall , where she is testifying on Mayor Katie Wilson’s first budget, which she called austerity. Wilson’s proposed 2027–28 budget would raise the Seattle Police Department’s spending by about $68 million, mostly due to union-negotiated wage increases.
“What kind of a socialist is that?” Henderson asked.
Blyth-Moss and Henderson are a couple, but they never set out to brand Squirrel Chops as an LGBTQ business.
“We didn’t start off as a lesbian coffee shop just because we are lesbian,” Blyth-Moss said. “But it’s definitely a queer chop shop.”
The salon specializes in gender-affirming haircuts, and Henderson credits barber Ali with bringing in trans clients who have since become coffee regulars.
“Especially in this political climate, people are looking for a safe place,” Henderson said. “We want this to be a space for everybody, and we mean that.”

Squirrel Chops opened as an early tenant in The Central , one of the first new buildings at 23rd and Union. The owners had wanted a funky old building, but older spaces came with higher rents and short leases ahead of demolition. Today the intersection is ringed by high-rises, in what Henderson calls the epicenter of gentrification in Seattle.

When the pandemic hit, Blyth-Moss moved the register to the shop’s street-facing window, and Squirrel Chops pivoted to takeout overnight. With the neighborhood working from home, business ran steady all day.

Blyth-Moss says she never thought the shop wouldn’t make it, but 2026 has been the hardest year yet. New building owners came in as the lease was ending, and the renewal turned into a struggle. Henderson said green coffee prices jumped about 120% after climate-driven poor harvests in Brazil and Vietnam.
Drip coffee has stayed near $3.75, even if it comes at a small loss for the shop.
“I want something that people can access,” Henderson said.
“If you go too high, people just won’t do it,” Sera Cahoone , a near 10-year veteran barista with Squirrel Chops added. “They’ll make it at home.”

The shop’s bean choices are political, too. Squirrel Chops dropped Slate Coffee to support workers after a walkout there. Retail bags now come from roasters including Stamp Act , and the house espresso comes from Thin Man , roasted by a longtime friend who got Henderson into coffee when she apprenticed at his bike shop. He now roasts essentially just for Squirrel Chops.

Over the years, the small space has hosted “tiny bench” concerts with Cahoone and other musicians, Friday happy hours, coffee-with-Sawant events, and a sign-making session ahead of the protests following Donald Trump’s first inauguration.

The pandemic paused much of that. Now a recent art show by barista Nazira has kicked off a revival, chef Becky Selengut will hold a cookbook signing in December, and “Gay Friday” is due for a comeback.
“It’s become that place where people meet people,” Blyth-Moss said.

Henderson and Sawant, friends since a 2009 marriage equality rally, now organize together in Workers Strike Back . Sawant finished third in August’s 9th Congressional District primary with about 13% 17.3% of the vote, though Henderson said she ran much stronger in the Central District. The group will keep pushing her campaign issues: ending U.S. military aid to Israel and stopping planned King County data centers.
For places like Squirrel Chops to thrive, Henderson said Seattle needs commercial and residential rent control, more public transit, and public healthcare and retirement programs.
“If your workers can’t afford to live in the city, what do you have?” she said.

Henderson’s last word for the neighborhood was a thank you. On one particularly bad day, she came into work to find a painting commissioned by a regular: a squirrel with a pearl earring, with a note saying the shop was a space the family treasured and was safe for their trans child.

“That, for me, was like, this is why we’re here,” Henderson said. “There is such a need for a safe space, a friendly space, a space that people can just gather outside their home, especially when everybody’s so lonely and isolated.”
Squirrel Chops is located at 2201 E Union. Its 10th anniversary celebration is planned for Friday, October 30th. You can learn more at squirrelchops.com .

articles.title: Free Will Astrology
articles.author: Rob Brezsny
paras: ARIES (March 21-April 19): For centuries, Japanese craftspeople have cultivated an ethos called shokunin kishitsu : a devotion to skilled work, lifelong learning, and continual refinement. The pursuit of perfection is less about reaching a final state than about bringing ever greater care and precision to the work. In traditional carpentry, this can mean years of learning to make joints whose quality resides in their strength and durability even though no customer will ever notice. I suggest you try out this attitude, Aries. Pour extra focus into details, regardless of whether anyone will applaud them. For Halloween, be a blacksmith, artisan, or eccentric inventor.

TAURUS (April 20-May 20): How do the oldest trees live for so many years? What’s their secret to longevity? They’re very adaptable. During storms, they bend without breaking. During droughts, they slow down their growth. Cultivating alliances with fungi is one of their brilliant tactics. You’re in an opportune phase to favor this approach to strength and endurance, Taurus. Here’s what I propose: Weave gleaming strands of buoyant resilience into your fervent willpower. Experiment with yielding strategically rather than resisting reflexively. Boost your soulful power through flexibility and adaptability. For Halloween, be an ancient oak tree, forest guardian, or mushroom spirit.

GEMINI (May 21-June 20): When archaeologists unearth a fresh batch of ancient artifacts, they never find a complete civilization in one dramatic moment. Each object or bone fragment helps explain another. A piece of pottery illuminates the meaning of an inscription. A broken staircase reveals why buildings were constructed as they were. Through educated guesswork and chains of association, knowledge accumulates. I invite you to wield your curiosity in the same way, Gemini. Treasure the sequence of little discoveries that gradually reshape your overall understanding. Have eager faith that every clue will lead you to further clues. For Halloween, be an archaeologist, paleontologist, or investigator of crime scenes.

CANCER (June 21-July 22): Researchers studying wolves have found that play remains essential to them throughout their lives. Mature wolves wrestle, chase, and invent games that strengthen trust and sharpen cooperation. They never graduate from joyful experimentation. I hope their friskiness inspires you to remember, dear Cancerian, that serious responsibilities don’t require a terminally serious personality. That’s especially crucial to keep in mind now. I invite you to bring maximum amounts of playful intelligence into everything you value. Laugh during challenging conversations. Invent rituals that nobody else would think of. Observe the true rule: Amused delight generates an atmosphere where meaningful work may become exceptional. For Halloween, be a playful wolf.

LEO (July 23-Aug. 22): Peacocks’ extravagant feathers are beautiful displays that also communicate health, vitality, and genetic resilience. They’re excellent role models for you. You should never apologize for expressing your charisma with style and theatrical flair. As long as your outer brilliance reflects inner vitality, your radiance will nourish rather than intimidate others. Authentic glamour is a public service. For Halloween, be a sun deity, lion monarch, or glamorous ringmaster.

VIRGO (Aug. 23-Sept. 22): “Dear Oracle: I am obsessed with improving things. I tinker with systems that already work fine. I wake at 3 a.m. and catalog details I could have done better. My results are never ultimate enough. Please offer tips to help me find rest. —Drooping Purist.” Dear Drooping: The autumn season is your teacher. The harvest is in; the fields are meant to lie fallow. Nothing more can be improved by force. Growth happens underground, invisibly. In that spirit, I invite you to practice the radical art of leaving at least one thing gloriously alone so it can work its magic outside the reach of your conscious awareness. For Halloween, be a scarecrow who stands serenely in the harvested field, watching over everything, accomplishing its whole purpose by being present.

LIBRA (Sept. 23-Oct. 22): If you’ve spent years regretting the moment a friend took credit for your best idea, that sting may finally lose its hold on you. If an opportunity you earned was handed to someone else, you may soon receive recognition in a form you never anticipated. And if an ancient family legend claims you were doomed to repeat the same mistake forever, you can now break that pattern. The days ahead favor overdue adjustments. Watch for turns of fortune that don’t erase what happened, but change what it means, and what becomes possible next. For Halloween, be an exorcist.

SCORPIO (Oct. 23-Nov. 21): This is your high holy season, Scorpio, which also happens to be the time when the veil is thinnest between this world and the other world. Others find this eerie, but you’ve always been at home here. You know how to explore the deepest depths, how to abide with what’s buried and hidden, and how to find treasure in the dark. In the coming weeks, your natural power to perceive what’s concealed will be amplified. For Halloween, be a psychopomp: a keeper of the threshold, a soul-guide draped in shadow and starlight who walks comfortably between the living and the dead.

SAGITTARIUS (Nov. 22-Dec. 21): Early balloonists had little control over the direction of their flights. They couldn’t steer horizontally. But they found that changing altitude allowed them to catch different winds moving in different directions. The smartest way to change course was to rise or descend. Keep that image close, Sagittarius. If you can’t alter external circumstances directly, shift your perspective or your social environment. A new current may be waiting higher or lower than where you’ve been drifting. For Halloween, be a hot-air balloon pilot, comet rider, sky pirate, or bird god like the Hindu Garuda.

CAPRICORN (Dec. 22-Jan. 19): Life must both perpetuate itself and surpass itself. Capricorn philosopher Simone de Beauvoir said that. We need continuity, but we also need transcendence. This beautifully encapsulates your assignment in the coming months. Your fun job will be to continue honoring the commitments that anchor your life while also making room for an exhilarating experiment or two. Make stability your launching pad rather than your destination. For Halloween, be the person you will be three years from now.

AQUARIUS (Jan. 20-Feb. 18): Inventors often describe breakthroughs arriving after weeks or months of seemingly unproductive tinkering. Clearly, their subconscious minds kept working on the puzzles even while their conscious minds felt frustrated. Eventually, a fresh arrangement appeared as if by magic. I suspect you’re approaching a threshold like that. Your experiments have been subliminally educating your intuition. The solution that’s searching for you may be cleverer than the one you’ve been searching for. For Halloween, be a time traveler, benevolent extraterrestrial, or eccentric professor.

PISCES (Feb. 19-March 20): Travelers crossing dark marshes on foot may report eerie, flickering lights hovering over the bog. Science explains these will-o’-the-wisps as gases from decaying matter that ignites in the night air. Folklore provides other theories: They’re spirit-lanterns, fairy lights, the lamps of the dead, or beckoning wanderers. I believe you’re in a similar liminal zone these days. Science and magic are both at work. Truth may take the form of both inexplicable mystery and fascinating anomalies that light your way. Be open to both! For Halloween, be a will-o’-the-wisp made flesh: a glowing spirit of the marsh draped in mist and lantern-light, beautiful and uncanny.

articles.title: Slog AM: Dolores Huerta Dies, a Deadly Spanish Train Crash, and ICE Renews Contract with Tacoma’s Northwest Detention Center
articles.author: Megan Seling
paras: Good morning, I guess : Sometimes, when it’s my turn to write Slog AM, I wake up around 6 a.m., open a browser and whisper to myself “please no bad news, please no bad news, please no bad news” while the headlines load. Without fail, though, someone great has died, an old war has taken a new, nasty turn, and the Trump administration has meddled in the upcoming election. This morning is no different. There continues to be bad news. So while you read this morning’s dread report, I recommend having the Smithsonian’s live cheetah cam open in another window. These babies are just three weeks old! Eeeeeee!!!!

GROSS. The US Immigration and Customs Enforcement just awarded a $1.5 billion 10-year contract to private prison company GEO Group to keep running Northwest Detention Center (NWDC) in Tacoma, the Seattle Times reports . GEO Group has consistently blocked efforts from the state Department of Health to investigate the NWDC’s conditions. This is the same detention center where more than 140 detainees went on a hunger strike to protest inedible food. I highly recommend following and supporting La Resistencia’s efforts . They’ve been trying to get this shit shut down for years.

A woman is dead after ChatGPT told her to go off her epilepsy medication. The New York Times reports that Bowen Wan, a Chinese immigrant who was living in Seattle when she died, began messaging ChatGPT when her epilepsy medication wasn’t working, and she had to take disability leave from her software engineering job at Amazon. After using the chatbot to help make sense of her health insurance and disability benefits, she started asking about her medication. The bot told her to taper her dosage. Even when she told it she was feeling worse, it responded, “Maintain 0 mg tomorrow… you must persevere.” It’s a horrifying and heartbreaking story about our country’s fucked up healthcare and insurance nightmare, our fucked up immigration system, and our fucked up lack of mental health resources. Read it, but have a pillow nearby to scream into afterward.

A Washington court ruled Monday “that a lawsuit taking aim at city rental regulations could move forward,” reports the Seattle Times . The suit from a local real estate investment firm alleges city tenant protection laws like limiting winter evictions and requirements that landlords not discriminate based on criminal records “destroyed” a building’s value. This puts Seattle’s tenant protection laws in jeopardy. The Seattle City Attorney’s office could appeal the decision, but chief of staff Dan Nolte told the Times , “We’re reviewing the decision and are meeting internally to discuss next steps. We haven’t made a decision on an appeal yet.”

Accused rapist wants anti-rape lawyer off his rape case. One of the men accused of participating in the alleged gang rape at Cornell University wants Attorney General Letitia James removed as special prosecutor on the case because she expressed support for Jane Doe on X and Facebook before being appointed to the case. This comes weeks after Trump said she should be off the case because she’s a “dirty and disgusting cop.” Calling it now: At least one of the seven accused rapists will end up with a job on Fox News, and another will be offered some token position in the Trump Administration.

RIP Dolores Huerta : Civil rights leader Dolores Huerta died at age 96 . Huerta co-founded the United Farm Workers (UFW) union in the midst of the historic five-year (!!!) Delano Grape Strike. Can you imagine striking for FIVE YEARS? After several more decades of fighting for workers’—and women’s and LGBTQ and immigrants’—rights, former President Barack Obama awarded Huerta the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2012. This March, she revealed that UFW’s co-founder, César Chavez, who died in 1993, sexually abused her for years. She never told anyone because she didn’t want it to tarnish their work. But let’s not talk anymore about him in remembering her. Her life’s work was also celebrated in 2019 here in Washington, when then-Governor Jay Inslee officially declared April 10 as Dolores Huerta Day .
Let’s break for something fun : Audrey, Julianne, and Dave got to go to the unofficial Gremlins museum (AND THEY DIDN’T INVITE ME!!!!!)

One more Stranger thing to throw on the pile : Please read this piece by Hunter Pauli about tax reform and how “the 99 percent and the 0.1 percent join hands to fuck the petit bourgeoise” if only for the very good accompanying artwork.
Nearly 70 people are dead after two high-speed trains crashed in Spain, causing some train cars to tumble down an embankment. The cause is still being investigated.

There’s still no clear winner in Israel’s election. According to NPR , 90 percent of the votes are counted, and “Israel’s election has reached a deadlock.” It’s the first election since the October 7 Hamas attacks. It’s between Benjamin Netanyahu, who has been Prime Minister for 13 years, and Gadi Eisenkot , a former head of the Israeli military, whose son was killed while fighting in Gaza. It could take weeks before a winner is chosen.

Trump’s election meddling has only just begun. As many predicted, Trump and his crooked bootlickers are attempting to discredit the midterm elections every chance they get. A federal judge in California just shot down Trump’s attempt to “segregate” about 20,000 ballots that Trump claims are “likely” not US citizens. The judge said this would “wreak havoc on the midterm elections.” The Justice Department also recently tried this shit here in Washington.

What are you doing tonight? How about a Halloween pre-funk with a night of death and hip-hop? The Stranger ’s own Charles Mudede will join Dr. Daudi Abe and Vitamin D to celebrate some of hip-hop’s greatest songs about death and grief. “Hip-hop’s birth occurred in and around urban communities shaped by socially imposed poverty, violence, and gun culture, and this dire situation, which is still with us today, resulted in a relationship between music and death that’s unique,” writes Mudede. If you saw these three do the same for love and hip-hop songs at the Clock-Out Lounge earlier this year, you know you’re in for a treat. Tickets are just $10 here . See you at the crossroads.

articles.title: Seattle Social Housing Developer Acquires Youngstown Flats, Adding 195 Homes to Portfolio
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: On Tuesday, the Seattle Social Housing Developer (SSHD) announced it is acquiring Youngstown Flats, a six-story apartment complex with 195 homes, located in West Seattle.

The property marks the recently funded public developer's second acquisition of an apartment complex. The SSHD's board granted a stamp of approval for the acquisition on Tuesday night. SSHD says it expects to buy Youngstown Flats for about $68 million and close on the property in mid-December.
Acquired at a cost of about $349,000 per apartment, the Youngstown Flats is significantly cheaper than building a comparable housing complex from scratch.

With the addition of Youngstown Flats, SSHD will own a total of 345 units. In May, the developer announced its first purchase : Elara at the Market, a 150-unit complex near Pike Place Market. That 2018 building was slightly newer, but in the same general age range that the developer appears to be targeting in its early acquisitions.

Earlier this month, SSHD announced its first construction project in the Central District, aiming to add 20 homes on a 7,000-square-foot lot purchased from the family of former House Speaker Frank Chopp, who passed away in 2025 after a long career as a champion for affordable housing at the state legislature. As a new construction project still in the design phase, those units will take longer to come online but are expected to open in 2028.

Youngtown Flats includes a broad range of unit sizes, which the SSHD pointed to as a selling point: "One of the central attractions of the complex were its large unit sizes. On average, each apartment is more than 800 square feet, and Youngstown Flats offers nearly 50 two-bedroom apartments." More recent apartment developments have tended to focus on one-bedroom units and to spurn multi-bedrooms, given current market realities.

“This is a tremendous opportunity for SSHD,” said the agency’s interim CEO Tiffani McCoy in a statement. “Providing permanently affordable, family-sized housing in different parts of Seattle is what we’re all about.”

Located at 4040 26th Ave SW, Youngstown Flats was developed by Barrientos Ryan and Legacy Partners. While a market-rate private development, the building participated in Seattle's Multifamily Tax Exemption (MFTE) program, which provided discounted rents to 20% of tenants in exchange for a property tax break. Since the building just passed the 12-year mark, SSHD noted it had aged out of MFTE, which was leading to rent pressure on residents in the formerly rent-restricted discounted units as the program lapsed.

"SSHD’s new ownership will potentially protect about 30 residents from economic displacement by offering them a permanent affordability program under the social housing model," the agency noted in a press release.

Excellent transit access was another attribute that SSHD underscored, pointing to two convenient nearby RapidRide bus lines: the H Line and C Line. The complex will also be a short walk from the Delridge light rail station planned as part of Sound Transit's planned West Seattle Link Extension, which will add 3.9 miles of service from SoDo to Alaska Junction in 2035 (following a series of planning delays) .

Given worries that light rail's arrival may drive up rents and displacement pressure on existing residents, social housing could provide an antidote to that dynamic, sheltering some housing stock from the whims of the market.

The complex is near the northern stub of the Longfellow Creek Legacy Trail, a hiking path through a greenbelt disrupted by West Seattle Golf Course, but continuing farther south. The Nucor steel mill is a few blocks north of the property, and a state driver's licensing office is next door.
Seattle Councilmember Rob Saka, who represents District 1 including West Seattle, celebrated the acquisition.

“I am so happy to see social housing being built in my district. Mixed-income communities, where those at lower incomes pay less in rent than those who make more, is an effective way of addressing Seattle’s housing and affordability crisis," Saka said in a statement. "And with transit-oriented development, residents can more easily reach work, school, and essential services.”

In 2024, Saka joined the centrist council majority in voting to put a competing measure on the ballot , which had the intent of blocking the excess compensation tax that will ultimately fund the Youngstown Flats acquisition and SSHD's other additions. Seattle voters ultimately rejected that council alternative and approved the grassroots "Prop 1A" measure in February 2025 – even in the face of opposition from then-Mayor Bruce Harrell and the Seattle Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce.
The high earners tax that Proposition 1A set in motion pulled in more revenue than expected, netting $115 million in its first year. That funding is what is powering the SSHD's buying spree.

Eventually, the SSHD plans to shift its focus to constructing new housing, rather than procuring existing apartment complexes. To get started, the acquisition strategy allows the SSHD to grow its portfolio quickly and establish collateral for loans to fund future construction projects.

Tenants at the Youngstown Flats may not notice a huge difference immediately, but they will have greater certainty their rents will not spike unexpectedly and the agency is planning some perks that market-rate landlords do not typically offer. Among them: free, one-year ORCA transit passes to all residents.

"We also plan to get rid of junk fees and freeze rents for existing leases for two years, through December 2028," the agency said. "Though not immediate, over the course of the first year of our ownership, SSHD will end Ratio Utility Billing System (RUBS) charges at the property, saving residents on utility costs as well."

The Youngstown Flats acquisition will allow the SSHD to exceeding its housing pipeline goal for 2026, the agency said, adding it expects to unveil additional acquisitions next year. By the end of 2027, SSHD expects to own more than 1,000 units of housing, meaning it expects to add at least 655 homes to its social housing rolls next year.
Correction : The original version incorrectly stated that Youngstown Flats has 193 homes, underselling by two units.
