articles.title: How the Federal Way Link Extension Impacted Bus Ridership Patterns
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: In December 2025, Sound Transit welcomed the first passengers aboard the Federal Way Link Extension. The three new stations on the 1 Line provide improved transit connectivity for many south King County residents. An accompanying bus service change in March 2026 improved frequency on many bus routes and adjusted a few bus routes to better connect with the new Link stations. While some routes lost ridership, many other routes welcomed new passengers. Link increased the total number of transit trips in south King County with nearly 10,000 combined weekday boardings at Federal Way, Star Lake, and Kent Des Moines stations.

This article will discuss the stop-level ridership data for select routes in south King County. To minimize the impact of seasonal changes in ridership, the analysis compares data from March-August 2025 with data from March-August 2026. The plots below show average weekday boardings and alightings at each stop, boardings are shown with positive bars, alightings are shown with negative bars. The different colors represent the number of passengers boarding/alighting during that time of day. The data for 2025 is shown as slightly faded. Click on each plot to open it in a new tab.

Route 181 serves as the primary east-west route between Federal Way and Auburn. Federal Way Transit Center has long been a busy stop as it connects passengers with many other bus routes. The new Federal Way Link station caused a 46% increase in Route 181 boardings at that stop each day, from 293 to 430 passengers. Overall ridership on Route 181 increased by about 114 passengers and the ridership at other stops was not significantly impacted.

Route 183 is a coverage route between Federal Way and Kent, via the new Star Lake station. Prior to the Federal Way Link Extension, the route connected to freeway bus routes 177, 193, and 574 at I-5 & 272nd St. That connection generated about 4 boardings per day for Route 183. Now, 71 passengers board Route 183 each weekday at Star Lake station, a 1,675% increase. This is still just a fraction of the 1,600 weekday Link boardings at the station as many Link passengers use the station’s 1,100 space parking garage. Both of the route’s termini, Federal Way and Kent, have a slight decrease in ridership. This may be from some passengers switching to Link at Star Lake rather than to another bus in Federal Way or Kent.

The A Line now runs in the 1 Line’s shadow between Federal Way and Tukwila. Thanks to fast and frequent service along Pacific Hwy, it was the most productive Metro route in 2024 . Now that Link offers a faster trip north from Federal Way, this title may be in trouble. Stops across the A Line have reduced ridership from 2025. At Federal Way Transit Center, boardings on the A Line have dropped 19%. Likewise, the number of passengers boarding the A Line at Pacific Hwy & 240th St (near Kent Des Moines station) has been cut in half. Part of this severe drop in boardings is due to the new A Line stop that opened next to Kent Des Moines station. When factoring in boardings at that stop, there is still a 24% decrease in A Line boardings near Kent Des Moines station. A similar change occurred at International Blvd & 200th St, next to Angle Lake station. Many passengers who previously rode the A Line to the Link 1 Line’s southern terminus in 2025 are now opting to board Link at one of the new stations. Despite this drop in ridership, the A Line still provides critical local service along Pacific Hwy. As the area continues to develop, ridership on the A Line will rebound.

Route 165 connected Burien and Des Moines with Kent and Auburn via the newly opened Kent Des Moines Link station. Since the new station opened, boardings on Route 165 at the nearby stops (Pacific Hwy & KDM Rd, KDM Station, Pacific Hwy & 240th St) have increased 50% (109 daily passengers). This increase is offset by 70 fewer boardings at Kent Sounder Station, suggesting some passengers have switched from Sounder to Link. The route’s termini both have slightly reduced boarding counts as well, likely also due to the new station. For instance, someone traveling between Normandy Park and downtown Seattle may have switched from the 165 + H Line to 165 + 1 Line for their trip. In August 2026, Route 165 was replaced by routes 164 and 166.

The Federal Way Link Extension also impacted a few Sound Transit Express bus routes. As these routes are operated by Pierce Transit, we do not have detailed ridership data for them (yet). Instead, this analysis will use the overall route ridership comparing April 2025 to April 2026.

Ridership on Route 574 increased about 10% year-over-year. This is mostly from more people traveling between Lakewood or Tacoma and Link in Federal Way. Route 574 previously connected with Link at SeaTac, so the FWLE likely did not attract too many new passengers. The August 2026 service change truncated Route 574 at Federal Way in exchange for a much needed frequency boost, which should further increase ridership.

Routes 577 and 578 form the primary bus connection between downtown Seattle and Federal Way. Most times of the day, these routes are still faster than Link for that trip. As a result, ridership has not changed too dramatically. Boardings are down 10% on both routes. Routes 577 and 578 both saw a more significant drop in ridership immediately after the FWLE opening in December, but ridership has since rebounded. Whether the recent ridership increases are due to the routes’ lower travel time or due to the World Cup and other seasonal ridership changes is still up in the air.

The Federal Way Link Extension is already making its mark on travel patterns in south King County. Local routes connecting with Link are busier than last year. Meanwhile, ST Express routes and the RapidRide A Line lost some passengers to Link. The August 2026 service change further improved local connectivity in south King County that should make transit the best option for even more trips.

While this article only covered a few routes, detailed ridership data for most King County Metro routes is now updated at seattletransitridership.com . In addition, the impact of the Crosslake Connection on bus routes in east King County was discussed in a recent article .

articles.title: How the Crosslake Connection Impacted Bus Ridership Patterns
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: On March 28, Sound Transit opened the much anticipated Crosslake Connection. This rail connection between Seattle and cities on the Eastside promised fast, frequent, and more reliable connectivity across Lake Washington. The Link 2 Line was designed to replace the hundreds of daily bus trips on I-90, freeing up service hours to improve local bus routes. Initially, however, the I-90 bus routes remained intact to offer extra capacity and redundancy during the World Cup. In the five months following the Crosslake Connection opening, passengers could either take the train or bus. Many chose to take the train. In August 2026, the 11 Link stations on the Eastside and Mercer Island accounted for 12,500 boardings each weekday.

This article will discuss the stop-level ridership data for select routes in east King County. To minimize the impact of seasonal changes in ridership, the analysis compares data from March-August 2025 with data from March-August 2026. The plots below show average weekday boardings and alightings at each stop, boardings are shown with positive bars, alightings are shown with negative bars. The different colors represent the number of passengers boarding/alighting during that time of day. The data for 2025 is shown as slightly faded. Click on each plot to open it in a new tab.
Sound Transit Express routes 550 and 554 provided all-day bus service across Lake Washington via I-90. Following the full 2 Line opening, many people switched from one of these routes to Link.

Overall ridership on Route 550 dropped 52% year-over-year. Boardings at the route’s busiest stop in 2025, Bellevue Transit Center, fell 57% as many passengers opted to take the 2 Line instead. Along Bellevue Way, the stop at 4th Street took the crown as the busiest stop with 278 weekday boardings (this stop had 366 weekday boardings in 2025). The other stops on Bellevue Way did not see significant changes in ridership. One stop that saw an increase in passenger boardings is South Bellevue station for Bellevue-bound trips. Passengers transferring from the 2 Line to Route 550 to access a stop on Bellevue Way doubled the boarding count to 50 per day. Route 550 stops near South Bellevue station and Mercer Island station. Seattle-bound boardings on Route 550 at those stops dropped by 78% and 74%, respectively.

Similar to Route 550, ridership on Route 554 fell where it overlaps with Link but remained constant elsewhere. Route 554’s stops in Issaquah had similar ridership to 2025. However, boardings at the Eastgate P&R (I-90 & 142nd Pl) fell 42%. This is likely due to more people choosing to use the nearby South Bellevue P&R and Link instead. On Mercer Island, the number of passengers boarding a Route 554 bus dropped 72% as many switched to the 2 Line. Route 554 was replaced by Route 556 in August. Route 556 provides more frequent service between Issaquah and Bellevue, via South Bellevue station and Bellevue Way.

State Route 520 is the only other connection between Seattle and the Eastside across Lake Washington. Some bus routes that use SR-520, such as Route 255, do not complete with the 2 Line and saw negligible changes in ridership patterns following the 2 Line opening. Other routes had significant changes as some passengers switched to the Link 2 Line.

While Route 545 takes a different route from Link across Lake Washington, it offers redundant service with the 2 Line between Redmond and downtown Seattle. Following the full 2 Line opening, ridership on the route fell 20%. At SR-520 & 40th St (near Redmond Technology station), inbound boardings fell 19%. Likewise, boardings at Redmond Transit Center dropped by 23%.

In downtown Seattle, Route 545 ridership has shifted north. Stops along Olive Way had a collective 2.5% increase in boardings, despite the closure of the peak-only stop at Boren Ave. Meanwhile, stops on 4th Ave had a collective 36% decrease in passenger boardings. This reflects passengers choosing to take the fastest trip. Route 545 is often faster than Link between the Denny Triangle and Redmond, while Link is usually faster between Redmond and CID or Pioneer Square. After all, Route 545 doesn’t save as much time as you think .

Compared to the 2 Line, Route 542 offers a shortcut between Redmond and the U District. A trip from the U District to downtown Redmond on Link takes 56 minutes vs just 32 minutes via Route 542. Ridership on this route has remained steady, with a 2.4% increase in boardings year-over-year. There were no significant changes to the route’s ridership patterns.

Route 271 also connected Seattle with the Eastside via SR-520. The long route had several noticeable changes in its ridership patterns following the opening of the Crosslake Connection. Trips between the U District and downtown Bellevue take 37 minutes on Link vs 24 minutes on Route 271. Despite the faster trip time on Route 271, the number of passengers boarding Seattle-bound trips at Bellevue Transit Center dropped 47%. This is likely from passengers who previously connected to another route in the U District and now have a more time-competitive option with Link (eg: trips from Bellevue to Capitol Hill).
Route 271 also had a 41% decrease in boardings at Eastgate Park & Ride. This is the same changed observed with Route 554 and is likely to due more people using the South Bellevue P&R instead.

The only new 2 Line station in Seattle, Judkins Park, impacted the ridership patterns of the five King County Metro routes that stop nearby: routes 7, 8, 9, 48, and 106. The intersection of an east-west Link station and five north-south bus routes is a key opportunity for many transfers. However, the data show that only 486 people are transferring between Link and one of the bus routes each weekday. This accounts for about ⅓ of boardings at Judkins Park station, a bit less than the projected 42% . The table below breaks down the bus boardings at Judkins Park station by route and direction.

The Crosslake Connection is already making its mark on travel patterns across Lake Washington. Many passengers switched from routes 271, 545, 550, and 554 to Link when it was the faster option. In Seattle, fewer people than expected are transferring between buses and the 2 Line at Judkins Park station.

The five month period of overlapping Link and bus service has come to a close and many bus routes were truncated in August . Seattle Transit Blog will share ridership data analysis from those changes in Spring 2027 (when the data are available).

In the meantime, explore detailed ridership data for most King County Metro, Sound Transit, and Community Transit routes at seattletransitridership.com . The dashboard has been updated to include stop-level data for all Metro and Metro operated Sound Transit routes from the Spring 2026 service change. The impact of the Federal Way Link Extension on bus routes in south King County will be discussed in an article tomorrow.

articles.title: The 38 Best Restaurants in Seattle
articles.author: <name>Sophie Grossman</name>
paras: “Where should I eat in Seattle?” Whether you’re a first-time visitor or a lifer, that question is seemingly simple but the answers are infinitely complex. Some of the main factors to consider are the type of food, price point, neighborhood, and occasion. That’s why Eater’s map of the 38 best restaurants in Seattle exists. This curated list of suggestions attempts to capture the diversity of the food scene in the Seattle metro area, from English pubs serving cumin-y lamb neck meat pies to Indian street food takeout spots, from classic French bistros to modern sushi bars, and so much more. Every place on the list has been open for at least six months, proving its merit.

Like many menus, this map updates every quarter — removal from the Eater 38 doesn’t mean a restaurant isn’t still awesome and won’t return in the future. New to the map as of October 2026: tamale and specialty coffee haven Cafetal Quilombo Cafe, Thai dumpling hotspot E-Jae Pak Mor, and Dim Sum King, which reigns supreme in counter-service dim sum.

A note on pricing: $ means entrees are mostly under $15; $$ means entrees are mostly under $25; $$$ means entrees are priced under $35; and $$$$ means entrees are more expensive than that, or it is primarily a tasting menu restaurant. (Prices are always subject to change.)

articles.title: The Best Restaurants in Seattle’s University District
articles.author: <name>Mark DeJoy</name>
paras: The University District is frequently (and wrongly) written off as a place only college kids would want to eat; the story usually goes that it’s rife with sketchy lunch counters, nondescript multinational fast food chains, and an overabundance of boba tea joints. But the truth is that the U District is one of the city’s essential dining destinations, with a dizzying array of global cuisines concentrated on its main street, University Way (confusingly known as the Ave).

There’s Korean food, regional Chinese specialties, Indian groceries, Vietnamese kitchens, falafel windows, and more on nearly every block. And practically everything is both affordable and genuinely good, so figuring out where to eat in this neighborhood is more a matter of grappling with the paradox of choice than anything else. So, here’s a short list to get you started.

articles.title: Cafe Lolo Is the Neighborhood Restaurant Every Neighborhood Deserves
articles.author: <name>Kat Thompson</name>
paras: If I were to describe the perfect neighborhood restaurant, Cafe Lolo would completely fit my definition. The food is comforting and nourishing, emphasizing local ingredients, which playfully come together in a way that feels both fresh and familiar. The space is draped in natural light that’s assisted by over a dozen lamps. The inviting dining room is covered in quirky Renaissance-inspired murals that don’t feel disruptive. There are to-go meal kits available for purchase, as well as local beers. It’s an atmosphere that invites you to unwind with a bottle of wine. Owners Leah Engel, Alex Halmi, and Brett Bankson are present, not only flitting about the room, but also cooking the dishes in the kitchen and laughing with customers. If I lived in the neighborhood, just off the main drag of Capitol Hill, it’s somewhere I’d want to return to over and over again.

Cafe Lolo has an extensive wine menu and many local beers, as well as bottles in the fridge you can pick up to-go. Although yes, the wine list — which includes just one glass from Washington, and more options from Oregon and Europe) — is worth perusing, the nonalcoholic tisanes are also made from seasonal ingredients. The strawberry rhubarb soda I had on my visit was effervescent and floral without an overpowering sweetness.

Like the rest of the menu, dessert will change pending seasons — but don’t skip it. My visit included a celebration of ripe, macerated strawberries over a semolina olive oil cake, which had a buttery crust and a tender interior crumb. There was also a scoop of rhubarb sorbet; light, sweet, and sharp.

articles.title: The Best Restaurants in Ballard
articles.author: <name>Mark DeJoy</name>
paras: Once a quiet working-class Nordic-American neighborhood, Ballard is now a nightlife, shopping, and restaurant destination. Boutiques and cocktail bars line Ballard Avenue (home to one of Seattle’s few year-round farmers markets ), and townhomes and high-rises have taken the place of single-family homes. Some of the best restaurants and bars in the city can be found here, along with almost (almost!) too many breweries , which is why if you walk far enough inland you can literally smell the hops. Where else in Seattle can you find Detroit-style pizza, Sri Lankan cocktails, and a congee specialist?
